summary: @better-auth/drizzle-adapter: Concurrent requests can exceed rate limits on PostgreSQL
description:
## Am I affected?

You are affected if you use `@better-auth/drizzle-adapter` from 1.6.17 through versions before 1.7.7 (including the 1.7.0 prereleases from beta.6 through rc.6) or stable 1.6.x releases of `@better-auth/kysely-adapter` from 1.6.17 onward, and keep rate-limit records in a PostgreSQL database. This also applies when you use the affected Drizzle adapter bundled with `better-auth`.

All of these must be true:

- Rate limiting is enabled.
- Rate-limit records are stored in the database.
- The database is PostgreSQL, used through one of the adapter versions above.

You are not affected if you store rate-limit records in memory (the default) or in secondary storage.

## Summary

Database-backed rate limiting on PostgreSQL can let a burst of concurrent requests go over the configured maximum. When many requests arrive at the same time, several of them can pass the limit check together. This weakens the rate limit on password sign-in, two-factor verification, one-time codes, password resets, and other rate-limited endpoints.

## Impact

An attacker who sends many requests at once can make more attempts than the application allows.

The issue does not bypass password or one-time-code validation. It does not directly compromise an account. The extent of the bypass depends on concurrent database requests, the number of application instances, and the rate-limit window.

## Patches

`@better-auth/kysely-adapter` is fixed in 1.7.0. Upgrade to 1.7.0 or later.

For Drizzle, upgrade `better-auth` and `@better-auth/drizzle-adapter` together to 1.7.7. No database schema or public API migration is required.

## Workarounds

- Store rate-limit records in secondary storage.
- Use a custom rate-limit storage that checks and increments the counter in one atomic step. An atomic step cannot be interrupted by another request.
- Enforce the intended limit at an upstream layer, such as a reverse proxy or gateway.

In-memory storage also avoids this issue. However, each application instance keeps its own counter, so it may not enforce one shared limit in multi-instance or serverless deployments.

## References

- [Drizzle guarded-update fix](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/11331)

summary: better-auth: OAuth state can be used as a Magic Link to sign in as another user
description:
## Am I affected?

You may be affected if you use `better-auth` from `1.4.0-beta.18` through versions before `1.7.7` with the Magic Link plugin and social or Generic OAuth sign-in.

You are affected if **all** of these are true:

- Magic Link is enabled with default `storeToken: "plain"`, or with `storeToken: "hashed"` and global `verification.storeIdentifier: "hashed"` (including a hashed default).
- At least one built-in social provider or Generic OAuth provider is enabled.
- OAuth state uses `account.storeStateStrategy: "database"`, the default when a database or secondary storage is configured.

Cookie-backed state blocks this path, subject to the OAuth Proxy condition below. With custom hashers, confirm the flows cannot resolve to the same stored identifier.

## Summary

In affected versions, Better Auth accepts an OAuth sign-in state value as a Magic Link token. An attacker can start an OAuth sign-in with any email address and use the returned state value to finish a Magic Link sign-in for that address. They never prove that they can read that email.

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker who knows a user's email address can get a normal session for that user, with all of that account's permissions. They need no access to the mailbox, and they do not need to sign in with the OAuth provider or complete an OAuth callback.

If Magic Link sign-up is enabled and no user has the email address, the attacker can instead create an account that Better Auth wrongly marks as email verified, and is signed in to it. The false verified-email flag can also bypass Better Auth's default unproven-account protections when the mailbox owner later signs in, leaving the attacker's session in that account. Applications that trust verified email addresses or email domains may give this account more access, depending on the application.

## Patches

Upgrade to `better-auth` 1.7.7, which fixes this issue. Keep installed Better Auth adapters, plugins, and integrations released alongside it on the same release version.

Upgrade servers sharing verification storage in the same coordinated cutover. Request new Magic Links and restart pending OAuth or SAML sign-in and account-linking flows that use Better Auth-generated state; links and state created before the upgrade cannot complete. For cookie-backed state, upgrade all nodes handling the same flow together. If you use OAuth Proxy, upgrade every participating production, preview, and development deployment together.

Update custom `verification.storeIdentifier.overrides` rules or storage integrations that inspect verification identifiers to match the `magic-link:` and `auth-state:` prefixes. Custom identifier hashers must preserve the purpose prefix in the value they hash. No database schema or user/account migration is required, and public token values and API signatures are unchanged.

## Workarounds

Until you upgrade to the fixed release, use one of these mitigations:

- Set `account.storeStateStrategy` to `"cookie"`. If you also use OAuth Proxy, first configure one dedicated OAuth Proxy `secret` across all participating environments that differs from each environment's global Better Auth secret. Cookie-backed state can expose a separate OAuth Proxy account-takeover path when the proxy shares the global secret and implicit account linking is enabled.
- Set the Magic Link plugin option `storeToken` to `"hashed"` **and** leave global `verification.storeIdentifier` unset or set it to `"plain"`. Global identifier hashing does not prevent this issue when Magic Link tokens are also hashed.
- Turn off Magic Link sign-in, or turn off social and Generic OAuth sign-in.

Setting `disableSignUp: true` on the Magic Link plugin is not enough. It only stops the creation of new verified accounts. It does not stop the takeover of existing accounts.

## References

- [Purpose-isolation fix](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/11494)
- [Better Auth Magic Link documentation](https://www.better-auth.com/docs/plugins/magic-link)
- [Better Auth OAuth documentation](https://www.better-auth.com/docs/concepts/oauth)
- [Better Auth Generic OAuth documentation](https://www.better-auth.com/docs/plugins/generic-oauth)
- [CWE-287: Improper Authentication](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/287.html)

summary: @better-auth/sso: Personal SSO providers can sign in as another provider's users
description:
## Am I affected?

You may be affected if you use `@better-auth/sso` `1.7.0-rc.2` through `1.7.0-rc.6` or `1.7.0` through `1.7.2`, and all of these conditions hold:

- An attacker can register a personal SSO provider or use one they registered earlier. Registration is enabled by default for signed-in users, with a limit of 10 providers each.
- Your application has not configured `resolveUser`.
- A victim's account is linked through another OpenID Connect (OIDC) or SAML provider, and the attacker can reproduce that provider's identity and the victim's account identifier.

Configuring `resolveUser` requires an exact provider match and blocks this path. Setting `providersLimit: 0` only stops new registrations; existing providers remain usable.

## Summary

The SSO plugin lets signed-in users register an OIDC or SAML provider. In affected versions, sign-in through a personal provider could match an account linked through a different provider and create a session for that account.

## Impact

An attacker with a Better Auth account can register a provider that copies a real provider's identity and reproduces a victim's user identifier. Better Auth then creates a new session for the victim's account without victim interaction.

The attack does not compromise the real identity provider or steal the victim's existing session.

## Patches

Upgrade `@better-auth/sso` to `1.7.3` or later. The fix prevents one provider from matching an account linked through another provider.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade now, block SSO sign-in at your application boundary until you can install the fixed release.

Setting `providersLimit: 0` prevents new personal-provider registration but does not disable providers that users already registered. If you keep SSO sign-in available, audit existing personal providers and remove any untrusted registrations. If you cannot verify that inventory, registration limits alone are only a partial mitigation.

If you already set `resolveUser`, the affected sign-in path requires an exact provider match. Upgrading is still the recommended fix.

## Technical details

Affected versions found linked accounts by the provider's issuer (the OIDC issuer or SAML entity ID) and the account identifier from the sign-in (the OIDC subject or SAML NameID). The lookup did not also check that the account belonged to the `providerId` that handled the sign-in.

An attacker could register a personal provider with the same OIDC issuer or SAML entity ID as a legitimate provider. The attacker still controlled the new provider's endpoints or signing keys, so it could assert the subject or NameID of an account linked through the legitimate provider. Because the lookup did not enforce the `providerId` boundary, Better Auth treated the victim's account as belonging to the attacker's provider and created a session for the victim. The assertion was valid for the attacker's provider, but it did not prove control of the legitimate provider's account namespace.

Version `1.7.3` restores account lookup using both the registered `providerId` and the asserted account identifier.

summary: better-auth: OAuth Proxy lets an attacker sign in as another user
description:
## Am I affected?

You may be affected if you use `better-auth` from 1.5.0-beta.12 through versions before 1.7.7 with the OAuth Proxy plugin. You are affected only if **all** of these are also true:

- On a participating environment, the OAuth Proxy plugin has no dedicated `secret`, or its `secret` equals that environment's global Better Auth secret.
- Sign-in state is stored in a cookie (`account.storeStateStrategy: "cookie"`). With a database or secondary storage, this is only the case if you chose it explicitly.
- Implicit account linking is on (the default).

You are not affected by this path if every participating environment uses a proxy `secret` distinct from its global Better Auth secret, if sign-in state is stored in the database, or if you use a version before 1.5.0-beta.12.

## Summary

In affected versions, the OAuth Proxy plugin trusts any user profile it can decrypt. In the affected setup, Better Auth encrypts sign-in state, including data the caller chose, with the same secret and hands it to anyone who starts a social sign-in. An attacker can use this to get a fake profile for another user's email address that the proxy accepts as real.

## Impact

An attacker without an account who knows a user's verified email address can sign in as that user, with that user's permissions. They can read private data, change the account, and link a provider account of their choice to it. They need no provider sign-in and no action from the victim. No availability impact is established, and a reported open redirect was not confirmed.

## Patches

Upgrade to `better-auth` 1.7.7, which fixes this issue. Keep installed Better Auth packages released alongside it on the same release version.

Upgrade all nodes handling the same cookie-backed OAuth or SAML state flow and all OAuth Proxy participants together, including the production coordinator and preview or development deployments. Mixed old and new participants cannot exchange state or proxy payloads. Restart pending sign-in and account-linking flows; pre-upgrade state cookies and proxy payloads are rejected. The existing `productionURL` and shared proxy `secret` configuration remain valid; this upgrade does not require rotating that secret. No database schema or user/account migration is required, and public options and API signatures are unchanged.

## Workarounds

Until you upgrade to the fixed release, apply one of these:

- Set one strong OAuth Proxy `secret` across every environment that takes part in the proxy flow, and keep it different from each environment's global Better Auth secret.
- Set `account.storeStateStrategy: "database"`. This is already the default when a database or secondary storage is configured. If Magic Link is also enabled, switching can expose a separate cross-purpose verification-record path in affected releases. Ensure the two flows resolve to distinct stored identifiers; with built-in options, use Magic Link `storeToken: "hashed"` with global `verification.storeIdentifier` unset or `"plain"`, or disable Magic Link or both built-in social and Generic OAuth sign-in.
- Remove the OAuth Proxy plugin if you do not need it.

Setting `account.accountLinking.disableImplicitLinking: true` stops this path from taking over an existing account. It does not fix the underlying flaw: the callback can still accept attacker-made data as a provider identity. Apply one of the steps above as well.

## References

- [Purpose-isolation fix](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/11494)
- [Better Auth OAuth Proxy documentation](https://www.better-auth.com/docs/plugins/oauth-proxy)
- [Better Auth OAuth state storage options](https://www.better-auth.com/docs/reference/options#storestatestrategy)
- [Better Auth account linking documentation](https://www.better-auth.com/docs/concepts/users-accounts#account-linking)
- [CWE-345: Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/345.html)
- [CWE-287: Improper Authentication](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/287.html)

summary: @better-auth/sso: Unproven domain claims can allow account takeover or organization joins
description:
## Am I affected?

You may be affected if you use `@better-auth/sso` `1.4.9` through `1.6.26`, `1.7.0-beta.0` through `1.7.0-rc.4`, or a `1.4.8` beta, and untrusted users can set up SSO providers. You are affected if either setup matches:

- **Verification off:** you use the organization plugin, leave SSO organization provisioning enabled, and leave `domainVerification.enabled` unset or false. An untrusted user can create or administer an organization and register its SSO provider.
- **Verification on:** you set `domainVerification.enabled: true`. An untrusted user can both verify and update an SSO provider they own or administer. You allow implicit account linking, or you assign organizations by verified domain.

You are not affected if only trusted operators can register, update, or verify SSO providers. Exact ranges per setup are in Technical details.

## Summary

The SSO plugin trusts a provider for the email domains it claims. Two flaws let a provider owner gain that trust for a domain they do not control. With verification off, organization assignment trusts unverified domains; with it on, a provider update during a verification check can mark an unproven domain as verified.

## Impact

**Verification off:** an attacker who controls an organization gets users added to it with the default role. This happens when a user with a matching email domain later signs in with a social provider. The attacker cannot sign in as that user or access their account.

**Verification on:** a signed-in provider owner can link an identity provider they control to an existing user's account, with no action from the victim. The attacker gains that user's data and actions. Where organizations are assigned by verified domain, the attacker can also add matching users to their organization.

## Patches

Upgrade `@better-auth/sso` to `1.6.27` on the stable line, or to `1.7.0-rc.5` on the `1.7` prerelease line.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade now, apply every step that matches your configuration:

- Stop untrusted users from registering, updating, or verifying SSO providers. Add your own authorization check before `/sso/register`, `/sso/update-provider`, and `/sso/verify-domain`.
- Set `account.accountLinking.disableImplicitLinking: true`. This blocks the account-takeover path.
- Set `organizationProvisioning.disabled: true`. This blocks automatic organization assignment.
- Review existing provider records. Remove domain claims from untrusted providers. Verify every domain again before you trust a provider that is already marked as verified.

Changing `domainVerification.enabled` alone does not fix both flaws. If you enable it, the domain-verification flaw is still reachable. If you disable it, the organization-assignment flaw is still reachable.

## Technical details

**Organization assignment trusts unverified domains.** This flaw affects `@better-auth/sso` from `1.4.8-beta.1` up to, but not including, stable `1.4.8`; stable `1.4.9` through `1.6.25`; and `1.7.0-beta.0` through `1.7.0-rc.2`. It requires both the SSO and organization plugins, SSO organization provisioning left enabled, and `domainVerification.enabled` disabled or unset. An untrusted user must be able to create or administer an organization and register an SSO provider for it. A user whose email address is in the claimed domain must later sign in through a social-provider callback that the SSO plugin handles.

An organization owner or administrator can register an SSO provider with any domain. When domain verification is disabled, the organization-assignment lookup does not require that domain to be verified. After the social sign-in, the SSO plugin matches the user's email domain to that provider and adds the user to the attacker's organization with the default role. Control of a provider record is treated as control of the domain it claims. The attacker can see the user's organization-member identity, and the default member permissions apply to the user.

**Domain verification can apply to the wrong domain.** This flaw was introduced in `1.5.0-beta.10`. It affects stable releases through `1.6.26` and the `1.7` prerelease line through `1.7.0-rc.4`. It requires `domainVerification.enabled: true`. An untrusted authenticated user must own a personal SSO provider or administer an organization-scoped provider, and must be able to reach both `/sso/verify-domain` and `/sso/update-provider`. The application must allow implicit account linking, or use verified SSO domains for automatic organization assignment. Implicit account linking means Better Auth connects a new sign-in to an existing account that has the same email address.

The verification endpoint reads the provider and its domains before it starts asynchronous DNS (Domain Name System) lookups. While the lookups are pending, the provider-update endpoint can change the domains and reset `domainVerified` to false. When the original lookup succeeds, verification matches the provider only by `providerId` and sets `domainVerified: true`. It never checks that the current domains passed the DNS check. The provider then carries a verified mark for a domain the owner never proved.

OpenID Connect (OIDC) and Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) callbacks trust a provider when `domainVerified` is true and the asserted email matches its stored domain. An identity provider controlled by the attacker can therefore assert an existing user's email and reach implicit account linking. Applications that use verified domains for organization assignment can also add matching users to the attacker's organization.

**The fix.** The patched releases enforce both domain-trust boundaries:

- Domain verification binds the final write to the same provider row, the exact stored domains that passed DNS verification, and a provider that is still unverified. If the provider changes during verification, verification fails and applies no stale proof.
- Automatic organization assignment requires domain verification to be enabled. It also requires a verified provider domain, a verified stored user email, normalized domain matching, and exactly one matching organization.

## References

- [CWE-287: Improper Authentication](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/287.html)
- [CWE-345: Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/345.html)
- [CWE-367: Time-of-check Time-of-use Race Condition](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/367.html)
- [CWE-862: Missing Authorization](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/862.html)
- [Affected domain-verification route](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/ea38fcac7435137604e9b3ba2fe149a1848d0eeb/packages/sso/src/routes/domain-verification.ts)
- [Affected organization-assignment helper](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/ea38fcac7435137604e9b3ba2fe149a1848d0eeb/packages/sso/src/linking/org-assignment.ts#L87-L175)
- [Affected SSO callback hook](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/ea38fcac7435137604e9b3ba2fe149a1848d0eeb/packages/sso/src/index.ts#L236-L258)

summary: better-auth: Attacker's password keeps working after magic link or email OTP sign-in
description:
## Am I affected?

This affects `better-auth` below 1.6.22, and `1.7.0-beta` releases below `1.7.0-beta.10`, when the magic-link or email-OTP plugin is enabled.

On those versions, you are affected if all of these are true:

- You enable the magic-link plugin or the email-OTP plugin.
- You also enable email and password sign-up with open registration.
- An account can exist for an email address before its owner first signs in with magic link or email OTP.

You are not affected if email and password sign-up with open registration is not enabled.

## Summary

Magic-link and email-OTP sign-in (a one-time code sent by email) do not remove a password that someone else set on an unverified account. An attacker can register with the victim's email address and a password of their choice. When the real owner later signs in with magic link or email OTP, the account becomes verified and the attacker's password starts to work.

## Impact

An attacker can gain lasting password access to the victim's account, at the same time as the victim. The attacker can read and change the victim's data, reset the credentials, and lock the victim out. The attacker needs the victim's email address. The takeover completes only when the victim signs in with magic link or email OTP.

## Patches

On the stable line, upgrade to `better-auth` 1.6.22 or later. On the 1.7 pre-release line, upgrade to `1.7.0-beta.10` or later. Earlier 1.7 betas, up to and including `1.7.0-beta.9`, still contain the bug.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade right away, two steps lower the risk:

- Require email verification before you accept any password on an account.
- Remove unverified accounts quickly, so that nobody can hold an email address for a long time.

These steps make the opening smaller, but they do not close it. Upgrading is the real fix.

## Technical details

This is a pre-account-hijacking weakness: an attacker creates an account for a victim's address before the victim signs up. It is the same class of flaw as the OAuth advisory GHSA-g38m-r43w-p2q7, but in the passwordless email flows.

The attack has three steps. First, the attacker uses open registration to sign up with the victim's email address and a password the attacker chooses. The account stays unverified, so the attacker cannot use it yet. Later, the real owner signs in with a magic link or an email OTP, which marks the account as verified. After that, the attacker's password works on the account.

When an account already exists for an email address, magic-link verification and email-OTP sign-in both sign in to that account. They mark the account as verified and create a session. Before the fix, neither flow removed a password that was set while the account was unverified. Neither flow revoked existing sessions. So a password set before anyone proved control of the mailbox kept working after the owner proved control.

Requiring email verification does not stop this. The verification step is the moment that turns the planted account into a usable one.

The fix treats current proof of control over the email address as the authority. When either flow finds an account whose email was never confirmed, it first removes the password and revokes existing sessions. Only then does it mark the account as verified and create the new session. The owner signs in as before. The fix removes only the access that was created before the owner proved control of the email address.

## References

- CWE-287: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/287.html
- CWE-345: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/345.html
- OpenID Connect Core 1.0, Section 5.7 (Claim Stability and Uniqueness): https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#ClaimStability
- Sudhodanan and Paverd, "Pre-hijacking Attacks on Web User Accounts", USENIX Security 2022: https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity22/presentation/sudhodanan

## Credit

Reported by the Vercel security team.

summary: better-auth: Device login approval does not show the requesting client or permissions
description:
## Am I affected?

You may be affected if you use `better-auth` from `1.3.8-beta.3` up to, but not including, `1.7.0-rc.3`, and you enable the `deviceAuthorization()` plugin. This range includes all 1.6 releases.

You are affected only if all of these are also true:

- An attacker can start a device request: `validateClient` is not configured, or the attacker can use a valid public client.
- Before allowing approval, your approval page does not show, from server-checked data, which client is asking and the exact permissions it requests.
- Users may approve a code or complete verification link they did not start and cannot compare with a device they have.
- Your application accepts the session token that the device flow returns, for example through the bearer plugin.

You are not affected if you do not enable the opt-in `deviceAuthorization()` plugin.

## Summary

The device authorization plugin lets a user sign in on one device by approving a short code on another. In affected versions, the approval information given to the user leaves out which client asked for access and which permissions it wants. The official approval examples therefore show only a generic request and a code, so users cannot tell their own device from an attacker's request.

## Impact

An attacker who convinces a signed-in user to approve the attacker's code receives a live Better Auth session token for that user. The attacker can then read or change any data the user's account can access. The attack needs the opt-in device flow, a request the attacker creates, and a user who actively approves it; it is not a sign-in bypass without user action.

## Patches

The fix first shipped in `1.7.0-rc.3`. Upgrade to `better-auth@1.7.0` or later. No 1.6 release contains the fix.

After upgrading, `GET /device` returns the requesting `client_id` and `scope` to the signed-in account that owns the request. If you built your own approval page, update it to show that client and those permissions, and keep approval disabled until they load.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade yet, do the following:

- Disable `deviceAuthorization()`, or block untrusted access to `/device/code`.
- Configure a strict `validateClient` allowlist. Do not rely on the allowlist alone: it limits who can start the flow, but it does not give users the missing approval information.
- Build your own approval endpoint. It should read the pending request from trusted server-side storage and map the checked client identifier to a trusted display name. Show the exact requested permissions and the user code. Keep approval disabled until this information loads.
- Tell users to reject device requests they did not expect. They should approve only when the same code is visible right now on a device they have.

## Technical details

A device starts the flow by calling `/device/code`. The plugin stores the client identifier and any requested scope with the pending request. Before approval, `GET /device` returns only the user code and its status. This is true even for a signed-in session of the user account that owns the request. An approval page built from that response cannot show which client asked for access or which permissions it wants. After approval, the original device code can be redeemed at `/device/token` for a Better Auth session token.

RFC 8628 describes this remote phishing scenario. It recommends that the server tell users they are authorizing a device and ask them to confirm that the device is in their possession. It also recommends showing device information that helps users detect impersonation. Client allowlisting reduces who can start the flow, but it does not give users the missing approval information. A valid public client can therefore still be affected when its identifier and requested permissions are not shown.

## References

- [RFC 8628 Section 3.3, User Interaction](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8628#section-3.3)
- [RFC 8628 Section 5.4, Remote Phishing](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8628#section-5.4)
- [CWE-451, User Interface (UI) Misrepresentation of Critical Information](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/451.html)

summary: @better-auth/sso: Four SSO flaws let an attacker sign in as another user
description:
## Am I affected?

You may be affected if you use `@better-auth/sso` 1.6.20 or older, or `1.7.0-beta.0` through `1.7.0-beta.9`, and users or organization admins can register their own SSO providers.

You are affected if all of these are true:

- Self-service SSO registration is on (`providersLimit` is greater than 0).
- You keep the default account linking (you have not set `account.accountLinking.disableImplicitLinking: true`).
- At least one flaw's condition applies: domain verification is on, an SSO provider that had linked accounts was deleted, SAML sign-in uses an identity provider that also serves other apps, or `saml.enableSingleLogout` is on.

You are not affected if users and organization admins cannot register SSO providers (`providersLimit: 0`).

## Summary

The SSO plugin can trust a sign-in for an identity it should not trust. Four separate flaws cause this: in domain verification, in deleting SSO providers, in SAML sign-in, and in SAML single logout. Each one lets an attacker sign in as another user, and one upgrade fixes all four.

## Impact

An attacker can get a valid session as another user. This is account takeover. In the domain verification, deleted provider, and single logout flaws, the attacker registers their own SSO provider. In the SAML sign-in flaw, the attacker needs no signing key. The victim does not need to act, except in the single logout flaw, where the attacker must lure the victim into triggering the logout. If the victim is an organization owner or admin, the attacker also gets those privileges.

## Patches

Upgrade `@better-auth/sso`:

- Stable line: upgrade to `1.6.21` or later.
- 1.7.0 pre-release line: upgrade to `1.7.0-beta.10` or later.

All four flaws are fixed in these versions.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade right away, these steps reduce the risk:

- Turn off self-service SSO registration (`providersLimit: 0`). Or require an admin to review each provider's `domain` and identity provider metadata before use.
- Turn off implicit account linking (`account: { accountLinking: { disableImplicitLinking: true } }`). This removes the linking step that the domain verification, deleted provider, and SAML audience flaws rely on.
- Check the `ssoProvider` table for verified rows whose `domain` contains `://`, `/`, `?`, `#`, or a comma. Check the `account` table for rows whose `providerId` has no matching provider. The upgrade stops new orphaned rows, but it does not remove old ones.
- For SAML, prefer pre-validated `defaultSSO` providers. Do not share one identity provider signing certificate across service providers when its assertions are not restricted to one service provider.
- Leave `saml.enableSingleLogout` off (the default) unless you need it.

## Technical details

Each flaw needs its own condition, listed with it below. An identity provider (IdP) is the service that signs users in. A service provider is an app that accepts those sign-ins.

**Domain verification can trust a domain you do not own.** This needs domain verification turned on. Two different parsers read a provider's `domain` value. One parser checks who owns the domain. The other decides which domains to trust at sign-in. A value that mixes a URL, a path, and a comma-separated list can pass the ownership check for the attacker's own domain. At sign-in, the same value also trusts the victim's domain. The attacker's IdP can then claim an identity on the victim's domain, and account linking attaches it to the real user. The fix requires DNS proof for every hostname a provider lists. URL, path, and comma input is now rejected.

**Deleting an SSO provider leaves its linked accounts behind.** Deleting a provider removes only the provider record. The linked `account` rows stay, and the provider's `providerId` becomes free to register again. A new provider that reuses that `providerId` and points to the attacker's IdP can then sign in to the old linked accounts, because trust is not checked again. Domain verification does not stop this. The fix deletes the linked `account` rows when a provider is deleted.

**A SAML assertion is not tied to this service provider.** A SAML assertion is the signed message an IdP sends to say who the user is. The SAML sign-in checks the signature, issuer, status, timestamps, and reuse. It does not check `AudienceRestriction`, `Recipient`, or `Destination`, the values that tie an assertion to one service provider. So when one IdP serves many service providers, a signed assertion meant for a different one is accepted. The attacker does not need a signing key. The fix checks the assertion's `Audience` against this service provider before it creates a session.

**Cross-site scripting (XSS) on the SAML single logout endpoint.** XSS means an attacker's script runs inside your site. This needs `saml.enableSingleLogout: true`. With single logout on, the logout handler builds a form that submits itself. The form's `action` address comes from the provider's registered metadata. The address is HTML-encoded, but its scheme is not checked. A `javascript:` or `data:` address therefore runs script in the auth origin. The endpoint needs no sign-in, skips origin checks, and accepts an unsigned `LogoutRequest` by default. An attacker who registers a provider with such a logout address can steal the session of a victim who is lured into triggering the logout. The fix allows only `http` and `https` addresses in the form `action`.

## References

- CWE-287 (Improper Authentication): https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/287.html
- CWE-345 (Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity): https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/345.html
- CWE-347 (Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature): https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/347.html
- CWE-459 (Incomplete Cleanup): https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/459.html
- CWE-79 (Cross-site Scripting): https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/79.html

summary: @better-auth/stripe: Organization billing actions can run on the wrong organization
description:
## Am I affected?

You may be affected if you use `@better-auth/stripe` 1.4.11 through 1.6.20, or 1.7.0-beta.0 through 1.7.0-beta.9, with organization subscriptions.

You are affected if all of these are true:

- Subscriptions are turned on (`subscription.enabled: true`).
- Organization subscriptions are turned on (`organization.enabled: true`), and you have set an `authorizeReference` callback.
- A user can belong to more than one organization, including one whose billing they should not manage.

You are not affected if you only use user subscriptions, or if organization subscriptions are turned off.

## Summary

Organization subscription actions can run on a different organization than the one the permission check approved. These actions are cancel, change plan, restore, and open the billing portal. When the two organizations differ, the action runs on the caller's active organization, which is the one selected in their session.

## Impact

A signed-in member can cancel, change the plan of, restore, or open the billing portal for an organization whose billing they may not manage. The target is always an organization the member already belongs to. Through the billing portal, the member can see that organization's payment methods, invoices, and subscription state.

## Patches

Upgrade to one of these patched versions:

- Stable: `@better-auth/stripe@1.6.21` or later.
- Beta: `@better-auth/stripe@1.7.0-beta.10` or later.

The fix reads the organization ID once, during the permission check, and the action uses that same ID. The approved organization and the organization the action changes are now always the same.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, make `authorizeReference` approve only the caller's active organization. Return `false` when the requested ID is not the active organization ID. Keep your existing role check as well:

```ts
if (referenceId !== session.activeOrganizationId) {
  return false;
}
```

This makes the approved organization and the active organization the same value.

## Technical details

Each organization subscription action runs in two steps. First, a middleware permission check reads the organization ID from the request body or the query string. It passes that ID to your `authorizeReference` callback. Second, the route handler runs the action. The handler reads the organization ID from the request body only. When the body has no ID, it uses the active organization from the session.

The query string causes the gap. The permission check can approve an organization ID that comes from the query string, such as one the caller may manage. The handler ignores the query string and uses the caller's active organization instead. So the check and the action can refer to different organizations.

## References

- CWE-639: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/639.html
- CWE-863: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/863.html

## Credit

Reported and fixed by Taesu ([@bytaesu](https://github.com/bytaesu)).

summary: @better-auth/scim: SCIM tokens can take over users they do not own, and deactivation fails
description:
## Am I affected?

You are affected if you use `@better-auth/scim` from `1.4.0-beta.27` through `1.6.21`, or from `1.7.0-beta.0` through `1.7.0-beta.9`. The deactivation and email-update problems need only the plugin and a valid SCIM token.

The provider-ID collision problem also needs all of these:

- Authenticated users can generate SCIM tokens.
- Your `canGenerateToken` policy is the default, or does not reject provider IDs that other sign-in providers already use.
- You use SSO, SAML, OIDC, generic OAuth, or social providers with custom provider IDs.
- Users already have accounts under those provider IDs.

You are not affected by the collision problem if your `canGenerateToken` policy rejects provider IDs that other providers already use.

## Summary

The SCIM plugin let a user create a SCIM token that reused the provider ID of an existing SSO, SAML, OIDC, generic OAuth, or social provider. The token could then manage that provider's users. Separately, SCIM deactivation reported success but left the user active, and SCIM email updates skipped the uniqueness check.

## Impact

An authenticated user allowed to generate SCIM tokens could list, read, and update users of a colliding provider. With a token not scoped to an organization, they could also delete those users. With an organization token, they could change the global profile fields of members created by the organization's colliding SSO or OIDC connection.

When an identity provider deactivated a user by sending `active: false`, the user could keep their sessions and access. SCIM email updates could give one user's email to another user on databases without a unique email index, which can break email-based login. On SQL databases, the update could fail with an unhandled error.

## Patches

Upgrade to `@better-auth/scim@1.6.22` or `@better-auth/scim@1.7.0-beta.10`. After the upgrade, application-level SCIM deactivation needs the admin plugin. Without it, the plugin rejects those deactivation requests instead of ignoring them.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade now, take these steps:

1. Configure `canGenerateToken` to reject provider IDs that match any account provider ID in your application. Include built-in providers, social providers, generic OAuth providers, and SSO, SAML, and OIDC provider IDs.
2. Restrict which users can generate SCIM tokens.
3. Check your existing `scimProvider` rows. Remove any row whose `providerId` matches the provider ID of another account provider.
4. If you use SCIM account linking, do not use broad linking rules based on email domain. A shared email domain does not prove that a SCIM token may manage an existing user. Use organization membership checks or an explicit check in your application instead.

These steps do not fix the deactivation or email-update problems. Until you upgrade, do not trust deactivation reports from your identity provider. Check that deactivated users have actually lost access, especially if your identity provider deprovisions users through `active: false`.

## Technical details

**Provider-ID collision.** The plugin used the same provider ID for two things: the SCIM provider configuration and the ownership of user accounts. When a user generated a SCIM token, the plugin did not reject every provider ID that other account providers use. The SCIM bearer middleware read the provider ID from the bearer token and loaded the matching `scimProvider` row. The user list and user lookup routes then searched ordinary account rows by `account.providerId`. This made the provider ID an authorization key that the user could choose. The SCIM user routes treated the colliding provider's users as SCIM-managed, even though the SCIM token never provisioned them.

With a colliding token, an attacker could list and read SCIM user resources for users linked to the colliding provider, and update their profile and account fields. For SCIM tokens not scoped to an organization, `DELETE /scim/v2/Users/:id` deleted the global Better Auth user and their sessions after it found the user through the colliding provider ID. A low-privileged authenticated user could therefore delete users linked to a colliding provider. For organization-scoped tokens, when the colliding provider ID matched the organization's SSO or OIDC connection, SCIM PUT or PATCH could find an SSO-provisioned organization member and change their global profile fields.

**Deactivation.** The SCIM user schemas and PATCH mapping did not include the `active` attribute. As a result, the plugin removed `active: false` from requests before processing them. Identity providers received a success response, but the user kept their identity, sessions, and access.

**Email updates.** SCIM PUT and PATCH updates changed a user's global email without the uniqueness check that SCIM create uses. They also left `emailVerified` unchanged after the email changed. On database adapters that do not enforce a unique index on email, SCIM could give one user's email to another user, which can break login and lookup that rely on email. On SQL adapters, the same update could raise an unhandled adapter error.

**Fix.** The fixed versions make these changes:

- Before a token is created, the plugin rejects SCIM provider IDs that collide with built-in providers, configured social providers, generic OAuth providers, or SSO providers.
- SCIM deletion removes only the SCIM account link when the user has other linked accounts. The plugin deletes the global user only when the SCIM account is the user's only linked account.
- The plugin supports the SCIM `active` attribute. For application-level deactivation, `active: false` sets the admin plugin's enforced disabled-user state and revokes the user's sessions. If the admin plugin is not installed, the plugin rejects the request instead of ignoring it.
- SCIM PUT and PATCH updates check that the new email is unique. When SCIM changes a user's email, the plugin resets `emailVerified`.

## References

- CWE-20 Improper Input Validation: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/20.html
- CWE-639 Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/639.html
- CWE-862 Missing Authorization: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/862.html
- SCIM 2.0 Protocol (RFC 7644): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7644
- OAuth 2.0 Bearer Token Usage (RFC 6750): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6750

summary: @better-auth/scim: Any signed-in user can take over another user's personal SCIM provider
description:
## Am I affected?

You may be affected if you use `@better-auth/scim` from `1.5.0` through `1.7.0-beta.3`, including every `1.6.x` release. You are affected if all of these are true:

- You create SCIM providers without an `organizationId` (personal providers).
- More than one user can sign in to your application.
- You have not set `providerOwnership: { enabled: true }`.

You are not affected if every SCIM provider belongs to an organization. Organization providers check membership and role.

## Summary

SCIM is a standard protocol that identity providers use to create and update user accounts in your application. By default, the SCIM plugin does not link a personal SCIM provider to the user who created it. As a result, any signed-in user can manage another user's personal provider.

## Impact

Any signed-in user can take over a personal SCIM provider that another user created. They need no organization membership and no special role. They can find and read the provider, create a new SCIM token for it, and delete the connection. A new token replaces the old one: the owner's token stops working, and the attacker can call the SCIM API for that provider. This includes managing users provisioned through SCIM, within the SCIM features you have enabled.

## Patches

The fix is in `@better-auth/scim@1.7.0-beta.4` and `1.7.0`. The `1.6.x` stable line is not patched; if you stay on it, use a workaround below.

This upgrade is breaking. The `providerOwnership` option is removed, and owner linking is always on.

1. Upgrade to `@better-auth/scim@1.7.0-beta.4` or `1.7.0`.
2. Run the schema migration: `npx auth migrate`.
3. Reclaim personal providers created before the upgrade. They have no owner, so no one can manage them. Either delete `scimProvider` rows that have neither `organizationId` nor `userId`, or set `userId` to the intended owner. Then create new tokens for those providers.

## Workarounds

Until you can upgrade, use one of these:

- Set `providerOwnership: { enabled: true }` when you register the plugin. Then update the schema so the `scimProvider.userId` column exists (`npx auth generate` or `npx auth migrate`). New personal providers are then linked to their owner, and other users are denied. This does not protect providers created before you turned on ownership. They stay without an owner until you recreate them.
- Always pass `organizationId` so every SCIM provider belongs to an organization. Organization providers check membership and role, so they are not exposed.
- Block access to the SCIM management endpoints at your network edge while personal providers still have no owner.

## Technical details

The SCIM management endpoints first shipped in `1.5.0`. Before the fix, the plugin tracked provider ownership with the optional `providerOwnership` setting and the `scimProvider.userId` column. Both were off by default. With ownership off, a new personal provider was stored without a `userId`. The access check for personal providers denied a request only when a stored owner existed and differed from the caller. A provider with no owner therefore passed the check for every signed-in user.

This gap reached every management operation: creating and re-creating tokens, reading a single provider, listing connections, and deleting a provider. The connection list returned every provider owned by the caller or with no `userId`.

Re-creating a token had the most impact. When a second user called `POST /scim/generate-token` with the `providerId` of an existing personal provider, the plugin deleted that provider, created a new one, and returned a new SCIM bearer token to the caller. The original owner's token no longer worked, and the new token authenticated against that provider's SCIM API routes.

The fix makes owner binding mandatory. `generateSCIMToken` records the creator's `userId` on every personal connection, and the management endpoints grant access only to that owner. Organization connections keep their existing membership and role checks. The `scimProvider.userId` column becomes a permanent part of the schema. Connections created before the upgrade have no owner and fail closed.

## References

- CWE-862: Missing Authorization: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/862.html
- CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/639.html
- SCIM 2.0 Protocol (RFC 7644): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7644
- OAuth 2.0 Bearer Token Usage (RFC 6750): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6750

summary: @better-auth/oauth-provider: Access tokens can target APIs the user did not authorize
description:
## Am I affected?

You are affected if you use `@better-auth/oauth-provider` on any stable `1.6.x` release (not patched) or a pre-release before `1.7.0-beta.4`, and **all** of these are true:

- You configure `validAudiences` with more than one audience, **or** you issue JWT access tokens whose audience your resource servers read. A resource server is an API that accepts the access tokens.
- Your resource servers decide what to allow based on that audience.

You are not affected by the cross-audience problem if you have a single `validAudiences` entry, or leave it unset so it defaults to your server's base URL. The provider then rejects any other audience. The gap with the specification still remains in this setup (see Technical details).

## Summary

The OAuth provider lets a client choose which resource server an access token is for. It does not check this choice against what the user authorized. It only checks that the resource server is on the `validAudiences` allowlist. Refresh tokens have the same gap.

## Impact

An attacker who can complete an OAuth flow for a registered client can get an access token for a resource server that the user's authorization did not cover. That resource server must be on the allowlist. If your resource servers use the audience to decide access, a token meant for one resource also works at another. The attacker stays limited to the scopes granted to that client, because the provider checks scopes separately from the resource.

## Patches

Fixed in `@better-auth/oauth-provider@1.7.0-beta.4`, and then in `1.7.0`. The stable `1.6.x` line is not patched. If you stay on `1.6.x`, use the workarounds below.

To upgrade:

1. Install `@better-auth/oauth-provider@1.7.0-beta.4` or later.
2. Run the schema migration with `npx auth migrate`. If you manage the schema yourself, run `npx auth generate` instead.

The fix is a breaking change:

- A token or refresh request can only narrow the authorized resources. A resource the authorization did not cover returns an `invalid_target` error.
- `customAccessTokenClaims` receives a `resources` array instead of `resource`.
- The fix adds a schema field, so the migration above is required.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade:

- Set `validAudiences` to a single audience, or leave it unset so it defaults to your base URL. The provider then rejects any other resource. This removes cross-audience selection, but the resource is still not tied to the authorization.
- Configure each resource server to accept a token only when its own identifier is the expected audience. Also reject tokens whose `aud` is an array that lists other audiences too.
- Do not treat the `resource` parameter as an authorization boundary until you run a release that contains the fix.

## Technical details

The client chooses the audience with the `resource` parameter (RFC 8707 "resource indicators"). The provider accepts `resource` only at the token endpoint (`/oauth2/token`), not at the authorization endpoint (`/oauth2/authorize`). At the token endpoint, it checks each requested resource against the server-wide `validAudiences` allowlist. It then writes the result into the `aud` claim of the JWT access token. It does not save the requested resources with the authorization code or with the refresh token.

For the authorization code flow, the provider ignores any resource the client sends at `/oauth2/authorize`. It accepts the resource sent at `/oauth2/token` on its own, checked only against the allowlist. For the refresh flow, the provider takes the audience only from the refresh request, because it keeps no resource from the original authorization. A refresh token from a flow for one resource can therefore return an access token for a different allow-listed resource. In both cases, the client picks the audience on each request. The audience is not part of what the user authorized.

With a single `validAudiences` entry, or the default base URL, a client cannot get a token for a different audience. The provider still does not tie the resource to the authorization in that setup, so the gap with the specification remains.

RFC 8707 expects a different behavior. The authorization server records the resources at authorization time. The token endpoint may then narrow them, but never widen them. A refresh token stays bound to the resources of the original authorization.

After the fix, the provider records the requested resources when the user authorizes and stores them with the authorization code. The token endpoint only allows a subset of those resources. The provider keeps the original resources across refresh, and it returns `aud` in token introspection responses.

## References

- RFC 8707, "Resource Indicators for OAuth 2.0", Section 2.2 "Access Token Request": https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8707#section-2.2
- RFC 9068, "JSON Web Token (JWT) Profile for OAuth 2.0 Access Tokens", Section 2.2 "Data Structure": https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9068#section-2.2
- CWE-863, "Incorrect Authorization": https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/863.html
- CWE-285, "Improper Authorization": https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/285.html

summary: better-auth: OIDC and MCP plugins accept javascript: redirect URIs that can run scripts
description:
## Am I affected?

Check this first: do you use the `oidc-provider` or `mcp` plugin with `better-auth` `1.6.12` or earlier, or with a `1.7.0-beta` build before `1.7.0-beta.4`?

If so, you are affected when **all** of these are also true:

- Your consent page runs in the browser.
- It takes the redirect URL returned by `authClient.oauth2.consent()` and navigates to it, for example by setting `window.location.href`.

You are **not** affected if **any** of these are true:

- Your consent flow ends with a redirect from the server, for example a Next.js or Remix server action.
- You copied the project's consent buttons demo without changes.
- You use `@better-auth/oauth-provider` instead of these plugins.

## Summary

The `oidc-provider` and `mcp` plugins do not check the scheme of the redirect URLs that an OAuth client registers. An attacker can register a `javascript:` URL, which holds script that the browser runs when a page navigates to it. A consent page that navigates to the returned URL then runs that script on your authorization server's origin.

## Impact

Anyone who can register an OAuth client can plant the URL: any signed-in user by default, or anyone when `allowDynamicClientRegistration` is `true`. A victim who approves the attacker's consent request runs the script with their own session, which can lead to account takeover. Better Auth itself never navigates to the returned URL, so the attack needs the consent page behavior above.

## Patches

Upgrade to `better-auth@1.6.13` (stable) or `1.7.0-beta.4` (pre-release). The fix checks the scheme of registered redirect URLs in both plugins.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, use one of these:

- **Check the URL on your consent page.** Before you navigate, parse the returned URL, for example with `new URL(redirectURI).protocol`. Navigate only when the scheme is `http:` or `https:`; otherwise, show an error. This blocks the attack no matter what the server returns.
- **Migrate to `@better-auth/oauth-provider`.** It checks redirect URLs when a client registers, supports MCP, and is the supported replacement for both plugins.
- **Keep `allowDynamicClientRegistration` at its default of `false`,** and limit who can register clients. This does not fix the issue, because any signed-in user can still register a harmful client. It only removes registration by people who are not signed in.

## Technical details

The attack is stored DOM-based cross-site scripting (XSS): the script runs because code in the browser navigates to it. Once it runs on the authorization server's origin, it can read `/api/auth/get-session`, call any session-scoped endpoint, and take over the account. The consent screen shows a client name that the attacker chooses, which makes the approval easier to trick. Risk is higher when ordinary end users, not only a restricted operator audience, can reach the consent page.

The `mcp` plugin is built on the same provider as `oidc-provider`, so it has the same flaw on the same versions. The `oidc-provider` plugin is deprecated, and the `mcp` plugin docs announce a move to `@better-auth/oauth-provider`. The deprecated status does not reduce the impact: both plugins are still published, importable, and documented. Users on affected versions cannot opt out without changing their integration, so the published versions stay exposed until users upgrade or migrate.

Client registration at `POST /oauth2/register` types `redirect_uris` as a list of any strings, with no scheme check. With the default `allowDynamicClientRegistration: false`, registration needs a signed-in session, and any signed-in user qualifies. With it set to `true`, registration needs no sign-in.

`GET /oauth2/authorize` compares the requested `redirect_uri` with the registered list by exact text match. So the registered `javascript:` URL matches itself and is saved in the consent verification record. When the user approves, the handler parses the URL with `new URL()`, adds the authorization code as a query parameter, and returns the result in JSON under the key `redirectURI`. The `javascript:` scheme survives this step unchanged.

The plugin documents the consent call, but not the redirect step that follows, and it does not warn that `redirectURI` can carry a dangerous scheme. A common way to finish the flow is to assign `redirectURI` to `window.location.href`, `location.assign`, or `location.replace`. When a page navigates to a `javascript:` URL, the browser runs its script in the current document's origin, which here is the authorization server. Browsers do not follow a `javascript:` URL delivered in a `Location` response header, which is why server-side redirects are safe.

The project's `consent-buttons.tsx` demo reads a `uri` field that the plugin never returns. Its navigation branch never runs, and it shows an error toast instead.

`@better-auth/oauth-provider` validates the same field with `SafeUrlSchema`. It rejects the `javascript:`, `data:`, and `vbscript:` schemes and requires HTTPS or a loopback host. The fix adds a matching scheme check to the `oidc-provider` and `mcp` plugins, which never had it; the field has been unvalidated since the registration endpoint was added.

## References

- CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting'). https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/79.html
- CWE-601: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site ('Open Redirect'). https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/601.html
- RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0) Section 3.1.2, Redirection Endpoint: the redirection endpoint URI must be an absolute URI. https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749#section-3.1.2
- MDN, javascript: URLs: navigating `window.location` to a `javascript:` URL runs the script body. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/URI/Reference/Schemes/javascript

summary: @better-auth/sso: Regular organization members can register SSO providers
description:
## Am I affected?

This affects apps that use `@better-auth/sso` `>= 1.2.10, < 1.6.11`, or a `1.7.0` pre-release from `1.7.0-beta.0` through `1.7.0-beta.3`, with the `organization()` plugin. You are affected if all of these are also true:

- `providersLimit` is at its default (`10`) or any other value above zero, so signed-in users can register SSO providers.
- An organization has members who are not admins, or your application can add users to organizations as regular members.

You are not affected if you set `providersLimit: 0` or do not use the `organization()` plugin.

## Summary

The SSO plugin lets any organization member register a new SSO provider (an OIDC or SAML identity provider) for that organization. It checks membership, but not the `owner` or `admin` role that listing, viewing, updating, and deleting these providers already require.

## Impact

A regular member can connect an identity provider they control to an organization they do not manage. Sign-ins through it can then add users to the organization, with the `member` role by default. If `organizationProvisioning` gives SSO users `admin` or a higher role, those users become organization admins without the owner's consent.

The risk is highest when people can join an organization without a direct admin decision (such as open invitations, self-serve onboarding, public team joins, or SCIM bulk imports), or when domain verification is off. Domain verification is off by default, so the new provider can be used at once.

## Patches

Upgrade to `@better-auth/sso@1.6.11` or later, or to `1.7.0-beta.4` or later on the 1.7 pre-release line. In the fixed versions, only an organization `owner` or `admin` can register a provider for that organization.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade now, use one or more of these steps:

- **Turn off SSO registration by users.** Set `sso({ providersLimit: 0 })`. Registration requests from users then fail with `FORBIDDEN`, before any membership check. Limitation: admins also cannot create providers themselves. You must create providers on the server with `auth.api.registerSSOProvider({ headers: serverAdminHeaders, body })`.
- **Turn off organization provisioning through SSO.** Set `sso({ organizationProvisioning: { disabled: true } })`. Limitation: a member can still register a provider. SSO sign-ins just stop adding users to the organization. Legitimate SSO onboarding also stops.
- **Add your own role check.** Add a `before` hook on `/sso/register`. The hook checks that the caller has the `owner` or `admin` role in the organization named by `body.organizationId`. This copies the fix into your own code.
- **Review existing providers.** Find `ssoProvider` rows that have an `organizationId`. For each row, check the role of its creator (`userId`) in that organization. Remove providers whose creator is not currently an `owner` or `admin`. Limitation: removing a provider does not remove the members it added. Review those members as a second step.

## Technical details

This issue does not rely on a separate documentation statement that only admins may create SSO connections. Better Auth already treats organization SSO providers as resources that only admins manage: the list, get, update, and delete endpoints in `providers.ts` check the caller with `isOrgAdmin`, which accepts the `owner` or `admin` role.

The registration endpoint, `POST /sso/register` (the `registerSSOProvider` handler in `sso.ts`), only looked up the caller's membership and never read `member.role`. So a low-privilege member could create a provider record that they could not view, update, or delete through the other provider endpoints. After registration, organization provisioning can add users asserted by the identity provider at `/sso/callback/{providerId}` to the target organization, at the role set by `organizationProvisioning.defaultRole` or returned by `organizationProvisioning.getRole`. When `domainVerification.enabled` is `false` (the default), the new provider is usable immediately.

The fix moves the role check out of `isOrgAdmin` into a shared `hasOrgAdminRole(member)` helper and applies it to registration. When a request includes `organizationId` and the `organization` plugin is enabled, the handler now requires the `owner` or `admin` role on the target organization. This matches the protection on the get, update, and delete endpoints.

summary: @better-auth/oauth-provider: Concurrent refreshes can create extra valid refresh tokens
description:
## Am I affected?

You are affected if you use the OAuth provider plugin in `@better-auth/oauth-provider` 1.6.0 up to, but not including, 1.6.11, or in `better-auth` 1.4.8-beta.7 up to, but not including, 1.6.0, and all of these are true:

- At least one OAuth client requests the `offline_access` scope, so your server issues refresh tokens.
- The same refresh token can be sent in two requests at the same time, by a client by accident or by an attacker who holds a stolen token.

You are not affected if no client requests `offline_access`.

## Summary

Each refresh revokes the old refresh token and issues a new one, and reuse of a revoked token should invalidate the whole token family. When two requests use the same refresh token at the same time, both can succeed. One refresh token then becomes two separate token families.

## Impact

Anyone holding a refresh token, such as an attacker who stole one, can split it into two families with the original user's authorized scope. Each rotation gives a fresh lifetime (7 days by default), so access can continue indefinitely, and revoking one branch does not stop the other. Reuse detection does not trigger when the legitimate user later refreshes.

## Patches

Upgrade to `@better-auth/oauth-provider` 1.6.11 or later. If you use the in-memory adapter, also upgrade `@better-auth/memory-adapter` to 1.6.11, or every refresh-token rotation fails.

In the fixed version, one of two competing refreshes succeeds and the other fails with `invalid_grant`. See Technical details for a known limit of the fix and an optional database constraint that `migrate` and `generate` do not add to existing installs. The fix does not depend on it.

## Workarounds

None of these workarounds fully fixes the problem. Upgrade if you can.

- **Database locking.** Run the OAuth refresh handler under serializable isolation, or lock the refresh-token row while it is updated (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`). This makes the problem harder to trigger, but does not remove it.
- **Short refresh-token lifetime.** Set `oauthProvider({ refreshTokenExpiresIn: 60 })` so that forked token families expire within one minute. This also makes user sessions shorter.
- **One refresh at a time in the client.** Use a lock (mutex) in your client code so that it sends only one refresh request at a time. This prevents accidental concurrent refreshes. It does not help against an attacker who has stolen a refresh token.
- **Disable refresh tokens.** Do not request the `offline_access` scope. This removes the problem, but it also removes long-lived sessions.

## Technical details

On the `refresh_token` grant at `POST /oauth2/token`, the server reads the `oauthRefreshToken` row, checks that it is not revoked, marks it revoked, and issues new tokens. These steps are not atomic. The replay-detection branch fires only when `revoked` is already set at read time, and concurrent requests both read the row before either revoke completes. The `adapter.update` that marks the row revoked matches on `id` only, not on `revoked IS NULL`, so both concurrent updates succeed (last write wins, no error). The schema has no unique constraint on `oauthRefreshToken.token`, so concurrent inserts do not collide either.

Concurrent use of one refresh token can happen in any of these ways:

- A single-page app shares one refresh token across browser tabs without a mutex.
- A mobile client retries after a temporary failure.
- A service worker queues requests made while offline.
- An attacker who has stolen a refresh token sends two requests at the same time.

RFC 9700 §4.14 calls for invalidating the refresh-token family when reuse is detected. The implementation tries to enforce this through the `revoked` check, but that check is not atomic with the step that consumes the token. A legitimate user whose token was forked does not trip family invalidation on refresh, because the attacker's branch has already swapped out the parent row the user's check reads.

The fix replaces the update in the rotation step with an atomic compare-and-swap: `UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND revoked IS NULL`, followed by a check that exactly one row changed. The losing request fails closed with `invalid_grant`, and the parent row stays revoked, so a later replay of the original token trips the existing family-invalidation guard. The explicit `revokeRefreshToken` path uses the same compare-and-swap.

`@better-auth/memory-adapter` 1.6.11 treats `undefined` and `null` as equal under an `eq null` predicate, matching SQL `IS NULL` and MongoDB's missing-or-null behavior. Without this change, the `revoked IS NULL` predicate never matches a row whose optional `revoked` field is absent, because the adapter factory does not write `undefined` fields that have no default. Rotation then fails on every call with the in-memory adapter.

Known limit: when reuse is detected during rotation, RFC 9700 §4.14 also calls for invalidating the winning request's tokens. The fixed version does not do this. It is deferred to a later minor release on the `next` channel, because it needs an opt-in transactional rotation in the adapter contract so that deleting the family cannot interleave with the winner's access-token insert.

Schema note: the fixed version adds a unique constraint on `oauthRefreshToken.token`, matching `oauthAccessToken.token`. The migration generator emits `UNIQUE` only for newly created columns, so `migrate` and `generate` do not add it to existing installs. The compare-and-swap fix does not depend on this constraint. The constraint is defense in depth: it makes duplicate tokens from a buggy custom `generateRefreshToken` callback fail loudly. If your tooling depends on it, add it manually:

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX oauth_refresh_token_token_uniq ON "oauthRefreshToken" (token);
```

## References

- [CWE-362: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization (Race Condition)](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/362.html)
- [CWE-367: Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/367.html)
- [CWE-294: Authentication Bypass by Capture-replay](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/294.html)
- [CWE-613: Insufficient Session Expiration](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/613.html)
- [RFC 9700 §4.14: Refresh Token Protection](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9700#section-4.14)
- [RFC 6749 §6: Refreshing an Access Token](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749#section-6)

summary: @better-auth/oauth-provider: Parallel requests can reuse one authorization code
description:
## Am I affected?

This affects apps that issue OAuth or OpenID Connect tokens with `@better-auth/oauth-provider` `>= 1.6.0, < 1.6.11`, or with an older OAuth provider plugin from `better-auth`.

You are affected if **all** of these are true:

- You use one of these:
  - `@better-auth/oauth-provider` `>= 1.6.0, < 1.6.11`.
  - The OAuth provider plugin built into `better-auth` `>= 1.4.8-beta.7, < 1.6.0`.
  - The legacy `oidc-provider` or `mcp` plugin from `better-auth/plugins`.
- Your token endpoint accepts requests from OAuth or OpenID Connect clients. Internal MCP clients count too, such as Claude Desktop, custom MCP tool callers, and AI agents.

You are not affected if a layer outside Better Auth already rejects a second use of the same authorization code. Examples are a load balancer cache keyed by the code, a database trigger that blocks a second token issue for the same code, or a custom adapter that deletes the code and checks the result in one atomic step.

## Summary

An OAuth authorization code must work only once. The token endpoint reads the stored code and deletes it in two separate steps. Two requests with the same code that arrive at the same time can both pass, and each one receives its own tokens.

## Impact

Whoever sends the same authorization code in parallel token requests can get several independent token sets from one user approval. Each set has an access token, a refresh token, and an ID token. All of them are valid for the scope the user approved. The normal single-use check does not stop the extra requests.

## Patches

Upgrade `@better-auth/oauth-provider` to `1.6.11` or later. If you use the legacy `oidc-provider` or `mcp` plugins, upgrade `better-auth` to `1.6.11` or later.

In the fixed versions, the first request takes the code and receives tokens. Any parallel request with the same code receives an `invalid_grant` error.

## Workarounds

None of these steps fully fixes the problem. Upgrading is the only good option.

- **Network layer:** Put a reverse proxy in front of the token endpoint that tracks the `code` values in use and handles requests for the same code one at a time. Examples are Envoy, NGINX with Lua, or a custom Cloudflare Worker. This is fragile when you run several instances, unless they share the tracking data (for example, in Redis).
- **Database layer:** Add a uniqueness rule so the database cannot create two `oauthAccessToken` rows from the same authorization code. This depends on your database adapter. It is not always possible, because the schema does not store the source code today.
- **Application layer:** Wrap `deleteVerificationByIdentifier` with a custom hook that uses `adapter.deleteMany` and checks how many rows it deleted. If it deleted no rows, reject the request with `invalid_grant`. This requires you to fork Better Auth's internal adapter.

## Technical details

The affected endpoint is `POST /oauth2/token` with the `authorization_code` grant. It is served at `/api/auth/oauth2/token`, and at `/oauth2/token` and `/mcp/token` for the legacy `oidc-provider` and `mcp` plugins, which share the same logic. The endpoint redeems the single-use code with a find-then-delete sequence that is not atomic. Two concurrent requests with the same `code` can both pass the read step before either delete completes. Both then continue to PKCE verification and `createUserTokens`, and each mints a fresh access token, refresh token, and ID token. RFC 6749 §4.1.2 requires authorization codes to be single-use.

The same pattern (find a single-use verification row, delete it, then trust the row) is used in 20 other places in the codebase. The delete step returns `Promise<void>` and discards the row count from `adapter.deleteMany`, so no caller can detect that another request already claimed the row.

The fix adds an atomic claim step to the internal adapter layer: `internalAdapter.consumeVerificationValue` deletes the row and returns its prior value in one operation. All three token endpoints now use it, and the highest-impact similar places move to it in the same release.

The fixed `@better-auth/oauth-provider` token endpoint also changes one error code. Its malformed-verification-value branches returned `invalid_verification`, which is not in the RFC 6749 §5.2 error set. Both branches now return `invalid_grant`, so spec-compliant clients can handle them without a special case.

## References

- [CWE-362: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization (Race Condition)](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/362.html)
- [CWE-367: Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/367.html)
- [CWE-294: Authentication Bypass by Capture-replay](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/294.html)
- [RFC 6749 §4.1.2: Authorization Response](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749#section-4.1.2)
- [OAuth 2.1 §4.1: Authorization Code Grant](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1#section-4.1)
