summary: @better-auth/sso: Any signed-in user can make the server fetch and read internal URLs
description:
## Am I affected?

You are affected if you use the SSO plugin from an affected `@better-auth/sso` version and let signed-in users register SSO providers. All of these must be true:

- Your version is `>= 0.1.0, < 1.6.11` on the stable line, or any `1.7.0-beta.x` pre-release.
- The `sso()` plugin is in your `betterAuth()` plugins.
- Any signed-in user can register an SSO provider (the default).

The account takeover in Impact also needs `sso({ trustEmailVerified: true })` and existing accounts whose email addresses are on domains the attacker chooses.

You are not affected if you do not use the SSO plugin.

## Summary

The SSO plugin lets signed-in users register their own OIDC identity provider. When a user enters the provider's endpoint URLs directly, the plugin does not check where they point. Your server then requests those URLs during sign-in and shows the response to the user.

## Impact

Any signed-in user can make your auth server request any address it can reach and read the response (server-side request forgery). This includes cloud metadata services, which can return full IAM credentials, internal-only APIs, and services bound to localhost. No other setting is needed.

With `trustEmailVerified: true`, the attacker can also take over existing accounts. Their provider can claim any email address as verified, and the sign-in is then linked to the existing account with that email.

## Patches

Upgrade to `@better-auth/sso@1.6.11` or later. It rejects endpoint URLs that point to non-public addresses unless their origin is in `trustedOrigins`.

If you run an identity provider on a private network on purpose, add its origin to `trustedOrigins` when you upgrade. Otherwise, that provider stops working after the upgrade.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade yet, use one or more of these steps:

- **Turn off provider self-registration.** Set `sso({ providersLimit: 0 })`. The plugin checks this limit first, so it blocks every `POST /sso/register` request, with or without `skipDiscovery`. Users can no longer register providers themselves.
- **Block the routes at a reverse proxy.** Block `POST /sso/register` and `POST /sso/update-provider` at the edge, or restrict them to a denylist of source IPs and a small list of admin users.
- **Limit outgoing network traffic.** At the firewall or VPC level, block requests from the auth server to private ranges (RFC 1918, RFC 4193), link-local ranges (`169.254.0.0/16`, `fe80::/10`), and cloud metadata host names. On AWS, also require IMDSv2 (`HttpTokens: required`).
- **Set `trustEmailVerified: false`.** This removes the account takeover. It does not stop the server-side request forgery.

## Technical details

`POST /sso/register` accepts the `oidcConfig.tokenEndpoint`, `oidcConfig.userInfoEndpoint`, and `oidcConfig.jwksEndpoint` URLs from the request when `skipDiscovery: true` is set. `POST /sso/update-provider` has the same behavior. The schema types these fields as bare strings, with no URL format check and no origin check. When `skipDiscovery` is `false`, the URLs go through `validateDiscoveryUrl`. When `skipDiscovery` is `true`, the plugin stores the supplied URLs on the `ssoProvider` row as they are. By default, any user with a valid Better Auth session can call `POST /sso/register`.

During the OIDC callback, three fetch sites read the stored URLs: `validateAuthorizationCode` for the token endpoint, `betterFetch` for the user info endpoint, and `validateToken` for the JWKS endpoint. The fetched response body is reflected back through the user profile, so the attacker reads the response rather than making a blind request. Reachable targets include AWS IMDS, the GCP metadata host name, and localhost services such as Redis or admin panels.

With `trustEmailVerified: true`, the attacker's user info response can set `emailVerified: true` for a chosen `email`. This triggers OAuth automatic account linking with any existing user row that has that email, which turns the SSRF into account takeover.

The fix applies to `POST /sso/register` with `skipDiscovery: true` and to every `POST /sso/update-provider` request. It validates `authorizationEndpoint`, `tokenEndpoint`, `userInfoEndpoint`, `jwksEndpoint`, and `discoveryEndpoint` at registration time. A URL is accepted only if one of these is true:

1. Its host is publicly routable, as decided by `isPublicRoutableHost` from `@better-auth/core/utils/host`. This rejects private ranges (RFC 1918), unique-local addresses (RFC 4193), link-local addresses (including the cloud metadata address `169.254.169.254`), loopback, multicast, broadcast, reserved ranges, and cloud metadata host names.
2. Its origin is listed in the application's `trustedOrigins` configuration. This keeps the documented option for identity providers run on a private network on purpose.

The schema for these fields also changes from `z.string()` to `z.url()`, so malformed URLs fail when the request is parsed instead of when the server fetches them.

## References

- [CWE-918: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/918.html)
- [CWE-20: Improper Input Validation](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/20.html)
- [CWE-441: Unintended Proxy or Intermediary](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/441.html)
- [CWE-345: Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/345.html)

summary: better-auth: OAuth sign-in can link to an account an attacker registered in advance
description:
## Am I affected?

You are affected if you run `better-auth` below `1.6.11`, or a `1.7.0` pre-release from `1.7.0-beta.0` through `1.7.0-beta.3`, and all of these are true:

- Email and password sign-in is on (`emailAndPassword.enabled: true`).
- You use an OAuth or SSO provider: a built-in social provider, `genericOAuth(...)`, or `@better-auth/sso`.
- `account.accountLinking.disableImplicitLinking` is not set to `true`.
- `account.accountLinking.enabled` is not set to `false`.

You are not affected if you set either of those two linking options. `emailAndPassword.requireEmailVerification: true` does not protect you.

## Summary

Better Auth can attach a first OAuth or SSO sign-in to an existing account with the same email address. This is called implicit linking. Before the fix, it trusted the provider's claim that the email was verified, but did not check that the existing account's email was verified.

## Impact

An attacker who knows a victim's email address can sign up with it and a password before the victim first signs in with OAuth or SSO. When the victim signs in, and the provider reports the email as verified, the victim's sign-in is linked to the attacker's account. The attacker keeps a working password on the account the victim uses, which is lasting access. The link also marks the email as verified, so `requireEmailVerification: true` does not block the attacker.

## Patches

Upgrade to `better-auth@1.6.11` or later, or to `1.7.0-beta.4` or later on the 1.7 pre-release line. These versions no longer links an OAuth identity to a local account whose email is not verified.

If your users sign up through OAuth and never verify their email locally, `account: { accountLinking: { requireLocalEmailVerified: false } }` keeps the old, less strict behavior. The option defaults to `true`, is deprecated, and is planned for removal in a later minor release, which will always apply the check.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade now, use one of these settings:

- Turn off implicit linking with `account.accountLinking.disableImplicitLinking: true`. Users can then link a new sign-in method only through the `/link-social` endpoint, while already signed in. Users can no longer add a sign-in method just by signing in with it.
- Turn off account linking with `account.accountLinking.enabled: false`. This closes the issue, but users can no longer use more than one sign-in method for the same account.

`emailAndPassword.requireEmailVerification: true` alone does not help.

## Technical details

The account-linking check in `handleOAuthUserInfo` accepts an implicit link when the provider's `email_verified` claim is `true`. It never reads the local user's `emailVerified` field. When no account matches the provider and provider account ID, the user lookup falls back to email. That lookup finds any account registered earlier at that email, for example through `/sign-up/email`, which creates a user with `emailVerified: false`.

After a link, a separate step sets the local `emailVerified` to `true` when the provider's claim is `true` and the local email matches the provider's email. This is correct for a real first-time link. Combined with the missing local check, it marks the attacker's account as verified, which is why `requireEmailVerification: true` does not mitigate.

Every sign-in path that goes through `handleOAuthUserInfo` is affected: built-in social providers, generic OAuth, OAuth proxy, SSO with OIDC, SSO with SAML, and one-tap. The `one-tap` plugin had its own simpler linking path; the fix applies the same check there.

In `1.6.11`, implicit linking also rejects a local user whose `emailVerified` is `false`. The Google ID token `email_verified` claim is now normalized, so the string `"false"` is treated as false. Earlier versions treated that string as true.

This is the pre-account hijacking class. It has the same shape as Microsoft "nOAuth" (2023) and the Sign in with Apple JWT flaw (2020).

## References

- [CWE-287: Improper Authentication](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/287.html)
- [CWE-345: Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/345.html)
- [Sudhodanan & Paverd, Pre-hijacked accounts: an empirical study of security failures in user account creation on the web (USENIX Security 2022)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity22/presentation/sudhodanan)

summary: better-auth: Deleted users stay signed in when sessions live in secondary storage
description:
## Am I affected?

This affects `better-auth` from 0.3.4 up to (but not including) 1.6.11, and `@better-auth/scim` from 1.6.0 up to (but not including) 1.6.11, when sessions are stored in `secondaryStorage`.

You are affected if **all** of these are true:

- You configure `secondaryStorage`, an external session cache such as Redis or a key-value store.
- `session.storeSessionInDatabase` is unset or `false`. This is the default.
- You delete users in **any** of these ways:
  - With the `admin` plugin: `auth.api.removeUser(...)` or `authClient.admin.removeUser(...)`.
  - With the `anonymous` plugin: its self-delete endpoint, or its automatic removal of the anonymous user after that user links a real account.
  - With `@better-auth/scim`: the SCIM delete user request.

You are not affected if `session.storeSessionInDatabase` is `true`, because deleting the user from the database also deletes the user's sessions.

## Summary

Some user deletion features remove the user but leave the user's sessions in secondary storage. Each stored session keeps its own copy of the user. Better Auth keeps accepting these sessions as valid until they expire, which is 7 days by default.

## Impact

A deleted user who holds a session from before the deletion stays signed in until that session expires (7 days by default). Until then, they can read and change everything they could before.

SCIM deprovisioning therefore does not end active sessions. An employee removed through SCIM can keep using the account for up to 7 days.

## Patches

Upgrade `better-auth` to 1.6.11 or later. If you use SCIM, also upgrade `@better-auth/scim` to 1.6.11 or later.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade now, use one of these options:

- **Configuration:** set `session.storeSessionInDatabase: true`. Sessions are then also written to the database, and deleting a user also deletes that user's sessions. This option increases database writes for sessions.
- **Admin plugin:** when you call `auth.api.removeUser`, also call `auth.api.revokeUserSessions({ body: { userId } })`. This removes the user's sessions.
- **SCIM:** in your SCIM provider's deprovisioning hook, call `auth.api.revokeUserSessions(...)` after the SCIM delete request.
- **Anonymous plugin:** in `onLinkAccount`, call `internalAdapter.deleteSessions(anonymousUser.user.id)` before the new session is issued.

## Technical details

Four deletion paths call `internalAdapter.deleteUser(userId)` without first calling `internalAdapter.deleteSessions(userId)`:

- The `admin` plugin's `removeUser` endpoint.
- The `anonymous` plugin's `/delete-anonymous-user` endpoint.
- The `anonymous` plugin's after-link hook, which deletes the anonymous user after an account is linked.
- The `@better-auth/scim` `DELETE /scim/v2/Users/:userId` endpoint.

The session payload in secondary storage carries a cached user object. It stays in place, so `internalAdapter.findSession(token)` keeps returning it, and `getSessionFromCtx` keeps accepting the session cookie until the session TTL elapses. The core `/delete-user` endpoint and its `/delete-user/callback` endpoint already delete sessions correctly.

In the fixed versions, all four paths call `deleteSessions(userId)` before `deleteUser(userId)`, so sessions leave secondary storage when the user row is removed.

## References

- [CWE-613: Insufficient Session Expiration](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/613.html)
- [CWE-672: Operation on a Resource after Expiration or Release](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/672.html)
- [CWE-459: Incomplete Cleanup](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/459.html)

summary: @better-auth/oauth-provider: clientPrivileges does not limit who can create OAuth clients
description:
## Am I affected?

You may be affected if you use `@better-auth/oauth-provider` before 1.6.5 and set `clientPrivileges` to control who can create OAuth clients.

You are affected if all of these are true:

- Your version is 1.4.8-beta.7 or later but earlier than 1.6.5, or the 1.7.0-beta.0 or 1.7.0-beta.1 prerelease.
- You set `clientPrivileges` and rely on it to limit who can create OAuth clients.
- Signed-in users you do not fully trust can reach the endpoints that create OAuth clients.

You are not affected if you do not set `clientPrivileges`; the bug then has no security effect.

## Summary

The `clientPrivileges` option decides who may manage OAuth clients, including who may create them. The endpoints that create OAuth clients skipped this check. So a deployment that used `clientPrivileges` to limit client registration was not actually limited.

## Impact

Any signed-in user who can reach the creation endpoints can register an OAuth client. That user chooses the client's redirect URIs (the addresses where users are sent after sign-in) and its other details. This makes phishing possible, because the client appears to users as a registered first-party application.

Only client creation is affected; other client actions were checked correctly.

The admin creation endpoint is server-only by design. If a deployment also exposes it to low-privilege users, which is a separate misconfiguration, those users can also set more sensitive client fields, such as whether the consent screen is skipped.

## Patches

Upgrade to `@better-auth/oauth-provider` 1.6.5.

The 1.7.0-beta.0 and 1.7.0-beta.1 prereleases are also affected. Upgrade to `@better-auth/oauth-provider` 1.7.0-beta.2 or later on the 1.7 line.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade now:

- Block the `/oauth2/create-client` and `/admin/oauth2/create-client` routes in your reverse proxy or middleware for every user who should not register clients.
- Do not expose the admin creation endpoint to end-user sessions. It is server-only by design. This step alone does not protect `/oauth2/create-client`.

## Technical details

The `clientPrivileges` hook documents a `create` action, but the `/oauth2/create-client` and `/admin/oauth2/create-client` endpoints did not call the hook before saving a new client. The other client operations (read, list, update, delete, and rotate) called it correctly.

The `/admin/oauth2/create-client` endpoint is marked `SERVER_ONLY`. When it is reachable by low-privilege users, they can also write sensitive fields, including `skip_consent`.

In 1.6.5, both create endpoints call the `clientPrivileges` hook with the action `"create"` before they save the client record.

summary: better-auth: Any signed-in user can approve or deny another person's device sign-in
description:
## Am I affected?

You are affected if you use `better-auth` at a version `>= 1.6.0, < 1.6.11` with the device authorization plugin enabled.

All of these must be true:

- Your `better-auth` version is `>= 1.6.0, < 1.6.11`.
- `deviceAuthorization()` is in your `plugins` array.

You are not affected if your application does not enable the `deviceAuthorization` plugin.

## Summary

The device sign-in flow did not check who owned a pending sign-in. It treated any signed-in user as the owner. So any signed-in user who knew the code for someone else's pending device sign-in could approve or deny it.

## Impact

An attacker with their own signed-in account can act on another person's pending device sign-in:

- **Take over the device session.** If the attacker approves, the device signs in to the attacker's account and then acts as the attacker.
- **Block the sign-in.** If the attacker denies, the real user's sign-in fails.

The attacker must learn the user code (the short code the device shows) before the real user completes approval. The device flow shows these codes to people by design, so they can leak in normal use.

## Patches

Upgrade to `better-auth@1.6.11` or later.

If you built a custom verification page, it must call `GET /device` with a signed-in session. Otherwise the sign-in does not complete.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade now, use one of these steps:

- **Disable the plugin** if you do not use the device flow. Remove `deviceAuthorization()` from your `plugins` array. This turns off the device flow.
- **Add a `before` hook** on `POST /device/approve` and `POST /device/deny`. The hook must record which session called `GET /device` for each user code. It must reject calls from any other session.
- **Shorten how long device codes stay pending** with the `expiresIn` plugin option. This makes the window for the attack smaller. It does not remove the flaw.

## Technical details

User codes can be seen over the shoulder, in a screen share, on a voice or video call, in a support-chat transcript, in referrer headers, or in shared logs.

The device flow links the waiting device to the user who enters the user code on the verification page. In affected versions, the plugin created this link only at approve or deny time. The `GET /device` verification handler did not claim the pending row. The ownership check on `POST /device/approve` and `POST /device/deny` skipped the check whenever the row's `userId` was unset, so it accepted any authenticated caller instead of rejecting the request.

The fix makes `GET /device` claim the pending row for the calling session. The approve and deny checks now require the row's owner to equal the calling session, and reject any other session.

RFC 8628 section 5.5 describes this type of risk as "Session Spying": a malicious party completes authorization before the real user who started the flow does.

## References

- [CWE-285: Improper Authorization](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/285.html)
- [CWE-863: Incorrect Authorization](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/863.html)
- [CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/639.html)
- [RFC 8628 section 5.5: Session Spying](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8628#section-5.5)

summary: better-auth: OAuth callback accepts a forged state value when state is kept in a cookie
description:
## Am I affected?

This affects applications that use `better-auth` below `1.6.2` and store OAuth state in a cookie (`storeStateStrategy: "cookie"`).

You are affected only if all of these are true:

- Your `better-auth` version is below `1.6.2`. This includes `@better-auth/sso` used with such a version.
- You set `storeStateStrategy` to `"cookie"`.
- At least one OAuth provider does not check a PKCE code verifier. This happens when either you set `pkce: false` on a `genericOAuth` provider, or you supply a custom `getToken` or `tokenUrl` that does not require the stored code verifier.
- Your provider returns arbitrary `code` values to the configured callback URL.

You are not affected if:

- You use `better-auth@1.6.2` or later.
- You keep the default `storeStateStrategy`, `"database"`.
- You use only the built-in social providers with PKCE turned on.

## Summary

OAuth sign-in sends a random `state` value to the provider and expects the same value back. This check protects users against cross-site request forgery (CSRF). With cookie storage, Better Auth checked that the state cookie was present and not expired, but not that the returned `state` matched it.

## Impact

An attacker who can make the victim's browser deliver an authorization code the attacker controls can do either of these:

- **Forced sign-in.** The victim's browser gets a session for the attacker's external account. The attacker can then see what the victim does in the application.
- **Persistent account linking.** In an account-linking flow, the attacker's external account is linked to the victim's signed-in account. The attacker keeps access until someone removes the link.

## Patches

Upgrade to `better-auth@1.6.2` or later.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade now, do either of these:

- Set `storeStateStrategy` back to `"database"`, the default. This closes the problem without a code change.
- Set `pkce: true` on every affected `genericOAuth` provider. The attacker cannot supply the matching code verifier.

## Technical details

In `parseGenericState`, the cookie branch decrypted the `oauth_state` cookie and checked its expiry. It did not compare the incoming `state` query parameter with the nonce that `generateGenericState` issued at sign-in. A callback to `/api/auth/oauth2/callback/<providerId>` with a forged `state` and any `code` was accepted while the victim's browser still held a live `oauth_state` cookie.

PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) ties the authorization code to the browser that started sign-in. Without it, nothing else binds the code to the victim's sign-in. This applies to `genericOAuth` providers with `pkce: false`, and to any custom `getToken` or `tokenUrl` path that does not enforce a round trip of the stored `codeVerifier`.

The `"database"` strategy was not affected. Its verification record is keyed by `state`, so the lookup itself requires a match.

The fix is in [PR #8949](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/8949) (commit `9deb7936a`, merged 2026-04-09). `generateGenericState` now writes `oauthState: state` into the encrypted cookie payload. `parseGenericState` rejects the callback when that stored value differs from the incoming `state`. The database branch also gained an explicit equality check as defense in depth.

The same state check serves every caller: generic OAuth, social sign-in, account linking, OAuth proxy passthrough, OIDC SSO, and SAML relay state. All of them receive the fix.

## References

- [PR #8949](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/8949)
- [Issue #8897](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/issues/8897)
- [CWE-352: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/352.html)
- [CWE-345: Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/345.html)
- [CWE-287: Improper Authentication](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/287.html)
- [RFC 6749 section 10.12: Cross-Site Request Forgery](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749#section-10.12)
- [RFC 7636: Proof Key for Code Exchange](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7636)

summary: better-auth: OIDC provider allows plain PKCE and lists unsigned tokens as supported
description:
## Am I affected?

You are affected if you use `better-auth` below 1.6.11 with the `oidcProvider()` or `mcp()` plugin enabled.

Each problem also needs its own condition. Any of these exposes you:

- **Unsigned tokens:** an application that trusts your server picks the signing algorithm from your discovery document instead of fixing one.
- **Plain PKCE:** the sign-in (authorization) URL is visible to some party other than the user's browser or app and your server.

You are not affected if you use only `@better-auth/oauth-provider` and have not enabled `oidcProvider()` or `mcp()`.

## Summary

The older OIDC provider plugins, `oidcProvider` and `mcp`, have two unsafe defaults. Their discovery document (the public `.well-known` file that applications read) lists `none`, meaning "no signature", as a supported token signing algorithm. They also accept the weak `plain` form of PKCE, the check that ties the end of a sign-in to the app that started it.

## Impact

An application that reads your algorithm list without fixing a real algorithm may accept tokens that have no signature. With `plain` PKCE, a leaked sign-in URL (for example in Referer headers, browser history, screen capture, or proxy logs) leaves the authorization code unprotected; `S256` protects it. These defaults also do not follow OAuth 2.1 or RFC 9700.

## Patches

Upgrade to `better-auth@1.6.11` or later. Clients that send a PKCE challenge must then also send `code_challenge_method=S256`. If older clients need `plain`, set `allowPlainCodeChallengeMethod: true`.

Both plugins are deprecated. When you can, move to `@better-auth/oauth-provider`, which has never listed `none` or accepted `plain` PKCE.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade now:

- **Turn off plain PKCE:** set `oidcProvider({ allowPlainCodeChallengeMethod: false })`, or the same option on `mcp`. This stops the server from accepting `plain`. The server still changes a missing `code_challenge_method` to `plain` before this check.
- **Remove `none` from the ID token algorithm list:** for `oidcProvider`, pass `metadata: { id_token_signing_alg_values_supported: ["RS256"] }`. For `mcp`, set the same value in `options.oidcConfig.metadata`. Check the result by requesting your `.well-known` address.
- **Move to `@better-auth/oauth-provider`:** it replaces the deprecated plugins and does not have either problem.

## Technical details

The affected plugins are `oidcProvider()` from `better-auth/plugins/oidc-provider` and `mcp()` from `better-auth/plugins/mcp`. The `mcp` plugin is built on `oidcProvider` and inherits both defaults.

**Unsigned tokens.** The metadata builders always add `"none"` to `id_token_signing_alg_values_supported` in the discovery document. The `mcp` plugin also adds it to `resource_signing_alg_values_supported` in its OAuth protected-resource metadata.

**Plain PKCE.** `allowPlainCodeChallengeMethod` defaults to allowing `plain`, so the authorize handler accepts `code_challenge_method=plain`. When a request has no `code_challenge_method`, the handler rewrites the missing value to `"plain"` before it checks which methods are allowed. So a client that leaves out the parameter still takes the `plain` path. Discovery advertises `code_challenge_methods_supported: ["S256"]`, which contradicts this behavior. RFC 9700 §2.1.1 (OAuth 2.1) forbids `plain`.

**The fix in 1.6.11.** Both plugins drop `"none"` from `id_token_signing_alg_values_supported`, and `mcp` drops it from `resource_signing_alg_values_supported`. `allowPlainCodeChallengeMethod` defaults to `false`, and a request with `code_challenge_method=plain` gets an `invalid_request` error unless the option is on. A `code_challenge` without a `code_challenge_method` is rejected instead of being rewritten to `plain`. By default, discovery and runtime behavior both support only `S256`. With `allowPlainCodeChallengeMethod: true`, a request without `code_challenge_method` is treated as `plain` again.

**`@better-auth/oauth-provider`.** Its metadata builder uses a `JWSAlgorithms` type that cannot contain `"none"`. Its authorize schema is `code_challenge_method: z.literal("S256").optional()`, which rejects `plain` when the request is parsed.

## References

- [CWE-327: Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/327.html)
- [CWE-757: Selection of Less-Secure Algorithm During Negotiation](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/757.html)
- [CWE-1188: Insecure Default Initialization of Resource](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1188.html)
- [RFC 9700 §2.1.1: PKCE](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9700#section-2.1.1)
- [RFC 9700 §2.1.2: Token Replay Prevention](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9700#section-2.1.2)
- [RFC 8414 §2: Authorization Server Metadata](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8414#section-2)

summary: better-auth: OIDC provider and MCP plugins accept refresh tokens without the client secret
description:
## Am I affected?

You may be affected if you run `better-auth` below 1.6.11 with the OIDC provider or MCP plugin. You are affected if all of these are true:

- Your `better-auth` version is below 1.6.11.
- You enable `oidcProvider()`, `mcp()`, or both.
- You have at least one confidential client, meaning a client that has a client secret.

You are not affected if all your clients are public clients that use PKCE, or if you only use `@better-auth/oauth-provider` without the `mcp` plugin.

## Summary

The OIDC provider and MCP plugins do not check the client secret when a confidential client uses a refresh token. They only check the refresh token and the client ID, which is public. A stolen refresh token is enough to get new tokens.

## Impact

An attacker who holds a valid refresh token and the client ID can act as the confidential client. They can keep getting new access and refresh tokens, with no time limit, until the refresh token is revoked. Each access token carries the scope the user originally granted. The attacker must first obtain a refresh token, for example from a database read, logs, cross-site scripting, or, for the MCP plugin, a script on another website.

## Patches

Upgrade to `better-auth@1.6.11` or later. Both plugins now require the client secret on refresh for confidential clients. Public clients do not change.

The `oidc-provider` plugin is still deprecated. When you can, migrate to `@better-auth/oauth-provider`, which checks the client secret on both grants by default and is not affected.

## Workarounds

None of these steps fully fixes the problem without the patch.

- **Migrate to `@better-auth/oauth-provider`.** It checks the client secret on both grants.
- **Make all clients public and require PKCE.** Set `type: "public"` on every client. When no client has a secret, the missing check does not matter.
- **Restrict network access to the token endpoints.** At your load balancer, allow only known client IP addresses to reach `/api/auth/oauth2/token` and `/api/auth/mcp/token`. This works for server-to-server flows. It does not work for clients that run on end-user devices.
- **Revoke refresh tokens if you suspect a leak.** Run the following to invalidate all refresh tokens for the affected client:

  ```ts
  db.deleteMany({ model: "oauthAccessToken", where: [{ field: "clientId", value: <id> }] })
  ```

- **For the MCP endpoint:** at an upstream proxy, remove the wildcard CORS header and allow only a short list of trusted origins.

## Technical details

The affected plugins are `oidcProvider()`, imported from `better-auth/plugins/oidc-provider`, and `mcp()`, imported from `better-auth/plugins/mcp`. A confidential client is any client with `type: "web"`, `type: "native"`, or `type: "user-agent-based"` in the `oauthApplication` table, or any `trustedClients` entry that does not have `type: "public"`.

RFC 6749 §6 and OAuth 2.1 §4.3 require a confidential client to authenticate to the token endpoint on every grant, including refresh. In the affected versions, the `refresh_token` grant of both plugins accepted the request based only on the stored refresh token and a matching `client_id`. The `authorization_code` grant of both plugins did check the client secret: the OIDC provider through `verifyStoredClientSecret`, and the MCP plugin through plain equality.

The plugins rotate refresh tokens, issuing a new one on each refresh. The refresh token row expires at `refreshTokenExpiresAt`, which defaults to 7 days, and each rotation refreshes that window. Each minted access token carries the original user's authorization scope, so the attacker can read or change whatever the resource server grants for that scope.

In 1.6.11, the refresh token grant uses the same constant-time comparison that the authorization code grant already used. Public clients have no secret to check, and PKCE protects their authorization code grant. The same release also fixes these related problems:

- The MCP plugin's `authorization_code` grant compared client secrets with `===` and ignored the `storeClientSecret: "encrypted"` and `storeClientSecret: "hashed"` settings. Both MCP grants now use `verifyStoredClientSecret`.
- The `/mcp/token` endpoint always sent `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, which made the refresh problem easier to abuse from a browser. The release removes this wildcard header and narrows the allowed origins, to match `@better-auth/oauth-provider`.
- The `Authorization: Basic` header parser now follows RFC 6749 §2.3.1. It splits the credential at the first colon and percent-decodes each half, so client IDs and secrets that contain reserved characters authenticate correctly.

`@better-auth/oauth-provider` routes both grants through `validateClientCredentials` and is not affected.

## References

- [CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/306.html)
- [CWE-287: Improper Authentication](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/287.html)
- [CWE-345: Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/345.html)
- [CWE-863: Incorrect Authorization](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/863.html)
- [RFC 6749 §6: Refreshing an Access Token](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749#section-6)
- [OAuth 2.1 §4.3: Refresh Token](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1#section-4.3)

summary: better-auth: Rate limiter can be bypassed by rotating IPv6 addresses
description:
## Am I affected?

You are affected if you use `better-auth` below `1.4.17` (or `1.5.0-beta.8` and earlier 1.5 prereleases) with the rate limiter on, and your app accepts IPv6 clients.

All of these must be true:

- Your version is below `1.4.17`, including `1.4.16`, or a 1.5 prerelease up to `1.5.0-beta.8`.
- The rate limiter is enabled (the default in production).
- Clients can reach your auth endpoints over IPv6. Most managed hosts allow this by default.
- The limiter reads the client IP from `x-forwarded-for` (the default) or another configured IP header.

You are not affected by address rotation if you do not use the rate limiter or serve only IPv4 clients.

## Summary

The rate limiter counted requests per exact IP address text. It did not group IPv6 addresses from the same network, and it counted different spellings of one address as different clients. So an IPv6 client can use a new address for each request and never hit the limit on sign-in, sign-up, password reset, or any other limited path.

## Impact

Anyone who controls a block of IPv6 addresses, which is common, can make unlimited authentication attempts. That speeds up password guessing, account discovery, and floods of password-reset and verification emails. The flaw removes one layer of defense. It does not directly compromise accounts: the attacker still needs a credential that the password store accepts.

## Patches

Upgrade to `better-auth@1.4.17` or later, or `1.5.0-beta.9` on the 1.5 prerelease line. The 1.6.x and 1.7.0-beta lines also include the fix. The fixed limiter treats each IPv6 `/64` block as one client; set `advanced.ipAddress.ipv6Subnet` if your clients get larger blocks.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade to `1.4.17`:

- **On `1.4.16` or later:** set `advanced.ipAddress.ipv6Subnet: 64` in your auth configuration. This gives the same behavior as `1.4.17` with the default configuration.
- **Below `1.4.16`:** apply the limit before requests reach Better Auth. In the rate-limit policy of your CDN, web application firewall, or load balancer, set the IPv6 prefix length to `/64`. Use a shorter prefix, which covers more addresses, if you serve residential traffic (see RFC 6177). Cloudflare, Vercel Firewall, AWS WAF, and Google Cloud Armor all support rate limits per prefix.
- **On any version, as a partial measure:** use `customRules` to set stricter limits for the sign-in, sign-up, and password-reset endpoints. This reduces the abuse but does not stop it.

## Technical details

Before the fix, `getIp` took the leftmost `x-forwarded-for` value (the default setup) or the configured IP header exactly as written, after one validity check. `onRequestRateLimit` then built the rate-limit key by joining that text with the request path. This affected `/sign-in/email`, `/sign-up/email`, `/forget-password`, and every other path the limiter protects. Two properties of IPv6 made the number of possible keys much larger than the number of real clients:

- Internet providers and cloud providers assign address blocks, not single addresses. RFC 6177 recommends `/56` blocks for home users. Cloud providers commonly assign `/29` to `/48` blocks. A client with one `/64` block already controls 2^64 source addresses without doing anything unusual.
- One IPv6 address can be written in several text forms: uppercase, compressed, IPv4-mapped, and IPv4 embedded in hexadecimal. RFC 5952 defines one standard form, but RFC 4291 section 2.2 still allows older mixed forms. An IPv4-mapped address in the `::ffff:0:0/96` range can be written with dotted decimal numbers or in hexadecimal.

Hosts that advertise IPv6 by default include Cloudflare, Vercel, Fly.io, AWS Application Load Balancer, and Google Cloud Load Balancing. With the bypass, credential stuffing and password guessing on `/sign-in/email` are no longer limited per client, account enumeration through differences in responses becomes faster, and password-reset and email-verification emails can be sent in much larger numbers.

The text-form problem can also reach deployments that serve only IPv4 clients, in rare edge cases: an upstream proxy can pass on an IPv4 source as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address.

The fix adds `normalizeIP` and applies it to every `getIp` result. It expands shortened IPv6 forms, converts hexadecimal digits to lowercase, converts IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses to plain IPv4, and applies a default `/64` prefix. After the fix, all text forms of one IPv6 address count as the same address, and an IPv4-mapped address counts as its IPv4 form. The rate-limit key now uses an explicit `|` separator between the address and the path, so that different address and path pairs cannot produce the same key.

Pull request #7470 added the normalization (`packages/core/src/utils/ip.ts`) and applied it to `getIp` and to the rate-limit key. Pull request #7509 changed the default IPv6 prefix length from `/128` to `/64`, so the default configuration is protected without extra settings. The `/64` default matches the smallest IPv6 block that providers commonly assign.

In `1.4.16`, `normalizeIP` already exists, but the default IPv6 prefix length is `/128` (one full address). No prefix mask applies with the default configuration, so address rotation still works. Setting `advanced.ipAddress.ipv6Subnet: 64` or upgrading to `1.4.17` closes it.

## References

- [CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/307.html)
- [RFC 4291: IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4291)
- [RFC 5952: A Recommendation for IPv6 Address Text Representation](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5952)
- [RFC 6177: IPv6 Address Assignment to End Sites](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6177)

summary: better-auth: Session cookie cache can let users skip two-factor authentication
description:
## Am I affected?

You may be affected if your application uses `better-auth` with two-factor authentication (2FA) and `session.cookieCache` both enabled. Versions 1.4.0 through 1.4.5 are affected, and 1.4.6 is the first fixed version.

You are not affected if `session.cookieCache` is off, or if you do not use two-factor authentication.

## Summary

Two-factor authentication asks for a second proof of identity after the first sign-in step. With session cookie caching on, a session can count as valid before the user completes that second step. The user may then reach signed-in routes without verifying the second factor.

## Impact

A person with valid primary credentials (the password or other first sign-in step) for an account that uses 2FA may access protected routes in your application without completing the second factor. This person can be an attacker or the account owner.

## Patches

Upgrade `better-auth` to 1.4.6 or later.

## Workarounds

- Disable `session.cookieCache` while you use two-factor authentication. This turns off session cookie caching. It is a temporary workaround, not a fix.
- Make sure session caching does not treat a session as fully signed in until all required steps, including 2FA, are complete.

## Technical details

When 2FA is enabled, Better Auth correctly detects that a user needs extra verification. It waits for the second factor before it treats the user as fully signed in. With `session.cookieCache` enabled, the session created at the first sign-in step may be cached as valid before 2FA verification. Later session lookups may return this cached session and do not check the 2FA requirement again.

cwes.name: Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel

summary: better-auth: Paths with repeated slashes can bypass disabled paths and rate limits
description:
## Am I affected?

You may be affected if you run `better-auth` before 1.4.5 and use `disabledPaths` or path-based rate limits.

You are affected if all of these are true:

- You use `better-auth` before version 1.4.5.
- You rely on `disabledPaths` or on path-based rate limits.
- Requests with repeated slashes in the path (for example `//sign-in/email`) reach Better Auth without change.

You are not affected if your platform or proxy collapses repeated slashes before the request reaches Better Auth. For example:

- Vercel with Next.js (it does this by default).
- Cloudflare, when [Normalize URLs to origin](https://developers.cloudflare.com/rules/normalization/settings/#normalize-urls-to-origin) is enabled.

## Summary

Better Auth can treat `/path` and `//path` as the same route. Because of this, a request with extra slashes in the path can get past `disabledPaths` and path-based rate limits.

## Impact

An attacker can call endpoints that you turned off with `disabledPaths`. An attacker can also avoid rate limits that apply to a specific path. What an attacker can do with a disabled endpoint depends on your configuration.

## Patches

Upgrade to `better-auth` 1.4.5 or later. This version includes the fixed routing library.

Also make sure that your proxy normalizes URLs.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade yet, collapse repeated slashes in the request URL before the request reaches the Better Auth handler. For example:

```ts
const req = new Request(...) // this would be the actual request object
const url = new URL(req.url);
const normalizedPath = url.pathname.replace(/\/+/g, "/");

if (url.pathname !== normalizedPath) {
  url.pathname = normalizedPath;
  // Update the raw request pathname
  Object.defineProperty(req, "url", {
    value: url.toString(),
    writable: true,
    configurable: true,
  });
}
```

## Technical details

Better Auth uses `better-call` for routing, and `better-call` uses the `rou3` router. Affected versions of `rou3` remove empty path segments. As a result, `/sign-in/email`, `//sign-in/email`, and `///sign-in/email` all match the same route. `better-call` depended on `rou3` version `^0.5.1`. The fix in `rou3` came after that version.

## References

- rou3 fix: https://github.com/h3js/rou3/commit/f60b43fa648399534507c9ac7db36d705b8874c3

Use of Non-Canonical URL Paths for Authorization Decisions

summary: @better-auth/passkey: Any signed-in user can delete other users' passkeys
description:
## Am I affected?

You are affected if your application uses an affected version of the Better Auth passkey plugin. This advisory lists `@better-auth/passkey` before 1.4.0 as affected.

No other setting is required. The risk is higher if you also set `useNumberId`.

## Summary

The passkey plugin lets a signed-in user delete a passkey by its ID. In affected versions, the server does not check that the passkey belongs to that user. As a result, one user can delete another user's passkeys.

## Impact

Any user with a valid session can delete any passkey in the application if they know or can guess its ID. The victim loses that passkey as a way to sign in. The attacker needs no other access.

With `useNumberId`, passkey IDs may be sequential numbers. An attacker can then guess IDs in order and delete every passkey in the application.

## Patches

Upgrade `@better-auth/passkey` to 1.4.0 or later.

## Technical details

The `POST /passkey/delete-passkey` endpoint takes the passkey ID from the request body (`ctx.body.id`) and uses it directly in the delete query. It trusts that value and does not first confirm that the passkey is owned by the user of the current session.

With `useNumberId`, passkey IDs may be auto-incrementing, which makes it trivial to delete all passkeys by enumeration.

summary: better-auth: The first request after startup can make every route return 404
description:
## Am I affected?

You may be affected if you use `better-auth` 1.2.4 through 1.4.2 and do not set `baseURL` explicitly.

You are affected only if all of these are true:

- Your `better-auth` version is 1.2.4 or later and earlier than 1.4.3.
- `baseURL` is not set in any way. For example, the `BETTER_AUTH_URL` environment variable is missing.
- An attacker can send the very first request to your server after it starts.

You are not affected if you set `baseURL` explicitly. In properly configured environments and on typical managed hosting platforms, this behavior cannot be reached.

## Summary

When no base URL is configured, Better Auth takes it from an incoming request. A request from outside can therefore set the wrong base path for Better Auth's routes. The base path is the URL prefix under which Better Auth serves its routes.

## Impact

An attacker who sends the very first request after the server starts can set a wrong base path. After that, all Better Auth routes return 404 (not found) for all users. This is a denial of service.

## Patches

Upgrade `better-auth` to 1.4.3 or later.

## Workarounds

Set `baseURL` explicitly, for example with the `BETTER_AUTH_URL` environment variable. Better Auth then does not take the base URL from incoming requests.

## Technical details

When `baseURL` is not defined through any other means, affected versions fall back to a value derived from an external request. The first request after startup can poison the router's base path this way. The fallback is only reachable when `baseURL` is not explicitly configured and the attacker makes the very first request to the server after startup.

cwes.name: External Initialization of Trusted Variables or Data Stores

summary: better-auth: Forged multi-session cookies can make sign-out delete arbitrary sessions
description:
## Am I affected?

You are affected if you use `better-auth` earlier than 1.4.0 with the multi-session plugin (`multiSession`) enabled.

You are not affected if you do not enable the multi-session plugin, or if you run `better-auth` 1.4.0 or later.

## Summary

The multi-session plugin lets one browser stay signed in to several accounts, with one cookie for each session. When a user signs out, the plugin deletes the sessions named in these cookies. It does not check that the cookies were signed by the server, so it also acts on forged cookies.

## Impact

An attacker can send a sign-out request with a forged multi-session cookie. The plugin reads the cookie value as a session token and deletes that session. This lets the attacker revoke arbitrary sessions, which signs those users out.

## Patches

Upgrade `better-auth` to 1.4.0 or later.

## Technical details

The issue is in the plugin's after-hook for the `/sign-out` route. Multi-session cookies have names that contain `_multi-`. The hook reads the raw values of these cookies and passes them directly to `internalAdapter.deleteSessions`. It does not verify the cookie signature with `getSignedCookie` or any equivalent check.

cwes.name: Reliance on Cookies without Validation and Integrity Checking

summary: better-auth: Anyone can create or change API keys for another user
description:
## Am I affected?

You are affected if you run `better-auth` 1.2.0 or later, earlier than 1.4.0, with the API key plugin (`apiKey`) enabled. Versions 1.3.26 through 1.3.34 fix key creation but not key changes, so they are still affected.

## Summary

The API key plugin can create and change API keys for the wrong user. Under certain conditions, the plugin trusts user details sent in the request as if they came from a signed-in session. This lets a request without a session act for another user.

## Impact

An attacker who is not signed in can create or change API keys for any user whose user ID they supply. An API key gives full signed-in access as that user. What follows depends on that user's privileges: it can include account compromise, access to sensitive data, or takeover of the wider application.

## Patches

Upgrade `better-auth` to 1.4.0 or later. No 1.3 release fixes key changes.

## Technical details

The flaw is in the fallback logic that decides who the current user is. When no session is present, the create and update handlers fill the user context from the request body. The plugin then uses that context for its authorization decisions. The server-side checks that protect privileged fields run only when authentication is required, so these fields are not protected. As a result, both the API key creation route and the update route accept requests without a session that target other users.

summary: better-auth: Organization invitations can be accepted by an unverified account
description:
## Am I affected?

You may be affected if you use the `organization` plugin of `better-auth` before `1.6.11`, or in `1.6.14` or later, and **all** of these are true:

- Users can sign in before they verify their email. The common case is `emailAndPassword: { enabled: true }` without requiring email verification before sign-in.
- You have not set `requireEmailVerificationOnInvitation: true` in the `organization()` options.
- Someone other than the invited person can get an invitation ID, for example from an admin screen, a forwarded email, or an invitation list shown to organization members.

You are not affected if **any** of these are true:

- A user whose email is not verified cannot get a usable session.
- You set `organization({ requireEmailVerificationOnInvitation: true })` for the affected invitation flows.

## Summary

The organization plugin lets a signed-in user act on an invitation when their email matches the invited email and they have the invitation ID. It does not always check that the email is verified. In apps that allow sign-in before verification, a person can sign up with the invited email address before the real mailbox owner accepts.

## Impact

A person with an unverified session for the invited email address can accept the invitation if they obtain its ID. This can give them organization membership that the organization did not intend to grant. Their access is limited to the role and permissions attached to that invitation.

## Patches

`better-auth@1.6.11` through `1.6.13` require a verified email by default for every invitation action by the recipient. That default blocked common sign-up flows from invitation links, so `better-auth@1.6.14` allows the normal emailed invitation flow again for invitation IDs that Better Auth generates.

Upgrading alone does not protect apps on `1.6.14` or later that meet the conditions above. Apply one of the workarounds below.

## Workarounds

Use one of these:

- Set `organization({ requireEmailVerificationOnInvitation: true })`. This requires a verified email before a user can act on an invitation by its ID.
- Require a verified email before sign-in, for example with `emailAndPassword.requireEmailVerification: true`. A user whose email is not verified then cannot get a usable session.
- Do not expose invitation IDs outside the invited mailbox. If your app shows organization invitation lists, add your own permission checks, or do not return invitation IDs that can be used to accept to users who should not have them.
- Add middleware to the organization invitation routes that rejects any request where the session user's `emailVerified` value is not `true`.

Apps should use the first or second option when any of these apply:

- They expose invitation IDs outside the invited user's mailbox.
- They show organization invitation lists to members.
- They use custom invitation delivery.
- They allow unverified email and password sessions for sensitive organizations.

## Technical details

The recipient invitation endpoints use `session.user.email` and an invitation ID to decide whether the current session can act on an invitation. The original report covered `acceptInvitation`, which checked that `invitation.email.toLowerCase()` matched `session.user.email.toLowerCase()`. A matching email string does not prove that the session owner controls the mailbox when the session email is unverified.

An invitation ID can reach someone other than the invited mailbox owner in many ways: an admin UI that shows the link, a link copied into chat, a forwarded email, a mailbox forwarding rule, a link preview, custom invitation delivery, or an organization-member invitation list that returns pending invitation IDs.

`better-auth@1.6.11` requires `session.user.emailVerified === true` by default for all four recipient endpoints: `acceptInvitation`, `rejectInvitation`, `getInvitation`, and `listUserInvitations`.

From `better-auth@1.6.14`, the default depends on how invitation IDs are created:

- `listUserInvitations` always requires a verified email, because it finds invitation IDs from `session.user.email`.
- `acceptInvitation`, `rejectInvitation`, and `getInvitation` do not require a verified email when Better Auth uses its built-in opaque invitation IDs. This includes the default ID generator and `advanced.database.generateId: "uuid"`.
- When invitation IDs are externally controlled or predictable, these three calls require a verified email unless the app sets `requireEmailVerificationOnInvitation: false`. This covers `advanced.database.generateId: "serial"`, `advanced.database.generateId: false`, and custom ID generation.

## References

- [CWE-287: Improper Authentication](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/287.html)
- [CWE-345: Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/345.html)
- [CWE-862: Missing Authorization](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/862.html)
- [CWE-441: Unintended Proxy or Intermediary](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/441.html)
- [PR #9877](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/9877)
- [Release v1.6.14](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/releases/tag/v1.6.14)

summary: better-auth: Trusted-origin check allows redirects to untrusted sites
description:
## Am I affected?

You are affected if you use `better-auth` 1.2.10 or earlier, or the 1.3.0-beta.1 pre-release, and your application serves any of these features:

- Email verification links
- Password reset links
- Account deletion confirmation links
- Magic link sign-in
- The OAuth proxy callback

## Summary

Before Better Auth redirects a user, it checks the destination against the application's trusted origins. In the features above, this check can be fooled. A URL passes when its text only begins with a trusted origin, even though it points to a different site.

## Impact

An attacker can create links to these features that send users to a site the application does not trust. This is an open redirect: the application's own address sends the user's browser to an outside site.

## Patches

Upgrade `better-auth` to 1.2.11 or later. If you use the 1.3.0-beta.1 pre-release, upgrade to 1.3.0-beta.4 or later.

## Technical details

The flaw is in the `originCheck` middleware, in its `matchesPattern` helper. For entries in `trustedOrigins` that contain no wildcard, the check compares the start of the URL text with the trusted origin (`url.startsWith(pattern)`). It does not compare the parsed origin. A URL that starts with the text of a trusted origin is therefore accepted, even when its host is a different site. Entries with a wildcard are matched against the URL's host instead.

The affected routes are `/verify-email`, `/reset-password/:token`, `/delete-user/callback`, `/magic-link/verify`, and `/oauth-proxy-callback`.

cwes.name: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site ('Open Redirect')

summary: better-auth: Trusted origin check can be bypassed, leading to account takeover
description:
## Am I affected?

You are affected if your application uses `better-auth` earlier than 1.1.21, or a 1.2.0 pre-release earlier than 1.2.0-beta.16. Version 1.1.20 contains only a partial fix.

The flaw is in the `trustedOrigins` check, which decides where Better Auth may redirect a user. It affects both kinds of entries in that list: absolute URLs and wildcard domain patterns.

You are not affected if you run `better-auth` 1.1.21 or a later stable release.

## Summary

Better Auth checks redirect addresses against your list of trusted origins before it sends a user there. An attacker can build a redirect address that passes this check but points to a site that is not trusted. This creates an open redirect: Better Auth sends the user to the attacker's site.

## Impact

An attacker who gets a user to click one crafted link can send that user to the attacker's site. Some redirects carry sensitive tokens in the address, such as password reset tokens. The attacker can receive these tokens and use them to take over the user's account. The attack works only if the victim clicks the crafted link.

## Patches

The fix is in `better-auth` 1.1.21. Upgrade to 1.1.21 or later. If you use a 1.2.0 pre-release, upgrade to 1.2.0-beta.16 or later.

## Technical details

The bypass is in the validation logic that compares a `callbackURL` value against the `trustedOrigins` list. A crafted `callbackURL` passes the origin check for both absolute URL entries and wildcard domain patterns. Redirect endpoints that include sensitive tokens, such as password reset tokens, then send those tokens to the attacker-controlled destination.

cwes.name: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site ('Open Redirect')

summary: better-auth: Callback URLs that start with // can send users to another site
description:
## Am I affected?

You are affected if you use `better-auth` before 1.1.20, or a 1.2.0 pre-release before 1.2.0-beta.15, and your application uses email verification or any other endpoint that accepts a callback URL.

## Summary

Better Auth can send users to a callback address after an action such as email verification. It blocks full external addresses, but it accepts addresses that start with two slashes, which browsers treat as another site. This lets a link send users outside your application (an open redirect).

## Impact

An attacker who gets a user to click a crafted email verification link can send that user to the attacker's site after the email is verified. The attacker can use this for phishing and credential theft, for example with a fake sign-in page, or for malware distribution. If the redirect is part of an OAuth flow, the attacker could receive authentication tokens on their own domain, which can lead to account takeover.

## Patches

Upgrade `better-auth` to 1.1.20 or later. If you use a 1.2.0 pre-release, upgrade to 1.2.0-beta.15 or later.

## Technical details

The email verification endpoint (`/auth/verify-email`) takes a `callbackURL` parameter and redirects the user there after successful verification. Other endpoints that accept a callback URL behave the same way. The server rejects fully qualified external URLs such as `https://evil.com`. It accepts scheme-less URLs such as `//malicious-site.com`, and browsers resolve these as `https://malicious-site.com`.

This flaw bypasses the fix for the earlier open redirect advisory GHSA-8jhw-6pjj-8723.

## References

- GHSA-8jhw-6pjj-8723: https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/security/advisories/GHSA-8jhw-6pjj-8723

cwes.name: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site ('Open Redirect')

summary: better-auth: Error page can run attacker JavaScript from a crafted link
description:
## Am I affected?

You are affected if you use `better-auth` 0.0.2 or later and earlier than 1.1.16. The flaw is in the error page that Better Auth provides.

## Summary

The Better Auth error page shows an error message taken from the link that opened it. Before the fix, it placed that text into the page as HTML without making it safe first. This let an attacker make the page run their own script, which is called reflected cross-site scripting (XSS).

## Impact

An attacker must get a user to open a specially crafted link to the error page. If the user opens it, the attacker can run any JavaScript in the context of that user's browser.

## Patches

The fix is in `better-auth` 1.1.16. Upgrade `better-auth` to 1.1.16 or later.

## Technical details

The error page is served at `/api/auth/error`. It reflected the value of the `error` URL parameter into the HTML response without escaping it, which allowed HTML injection. The affected code is in [`packages/better-auth/src/api/routes/error.ts`](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/blob/05ada0b79dbcac93cc04ceb79b23ca598d07830c/packages/better-auth/src/api/routes/error.ts#L81).

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')
